docs.title: go-pki-est
docs.text:
go-pki-est is a Go library for Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), the certificate enrollment protocol of RFC 7030. It contains:

  • an EST client for Go programs, est.Client
  • an EST server as an http.Handler in front of your CA, built by est.NewRouter from your implementation of the CA interface
  • estclient, a command line client built on the library
  • estserver, a test server with a mock CA for development

Clients sign in with TLS client certificates, HTTP Basic, bearer tokens or TLS-SRP passwords. Certificates can carry post-quantum ML-DSA keys. The support matrix lists what is covered.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est

The module needs Go 1.27.3 or newer. The package is imported as est. The command line tools install with:

go install github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est/cmd/estclient@latest

go install github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est/cmd/estserver@latest

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: go-pki-est is a protocol layer. The client turns Go calls into EST requests. The server turns EST requests into calls to a CA interface that your application implements. TLS, the CA itself, the decision who may enroll and any storage stay with your application.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Client[est.Client or another EST client] -->|TLS or TLS-SRP| Listener[Host TLS listener]
  Listener --> Router[Router from NewRouter]
  Router --> Hooks[Authentication and check hooks]
  Router --> Refusals[RefusalRecorder]
  Router --> CA[Host CA]
Component Provided by Role est.Client Library Connects, signs in and runs one EST operation per call TLS listener Host Terminates TLS or TLS-SRP and requests client certificates Router Library, built by NewRouter Checks and decodes requests, checks renewals and encodes responses CA Host Returns CA certificates and CSR attributes and issues certificates CheckBasicAuth, CheckBearerToken Host, optional Decide who may enroll CheckCSRSignature, VerifyClientCertificate Host, optional Replace signature checks that crypto/x509 cannot do RefusalRecorder Host, optional Receives the requests the router refuses itself Logger Host, optional Receives one entry per request and the server errors

The router is a plain http.Handler. You serve it with your own http.Server, next to other handlers if you like. It reads the TLS state from http.Request.TLS and the TLS-SRP username from the request context, where your listener puts it with WithSRPUsername.

docs.title: Request handling on the server
docs.text:
Every request passes these steps in order. A step that refuses the request answers at once.

  1. A timeout of ServerConfig.Timeout, 60 seconds by default, bounds the request context.
  2. A request ID is assigned. With TrustProxyHeaders the client address comes from X-Real-IP or X-Forwarded-For.
  3. The request is logged when it completes. A panic in a handler or in the CA is recovered, logged with its stack and answered with 500.
  4. The Server, Strict-Transport-Security and X-Content-Type-Options headers are set.
  5. With AllowedHosts, the Host header must name an allowed host.
  6. The body is limited to MaxRequestBody, 64 KiB by default.
  7. With RateLimit, a shared rate limiter answers 429 when it is empty.
  8. An additional path segment longer than 255 bytes answers 414.
  9. For POST operations the content type must match the operation.
  10. For POST operations and /healthcheck, authentication runs CheckBearerToken or CheckBasicAuth. See Authentication.
  11. The operation decodes the body, parses the CSR and checks its signature.
  12. For /simplereenroll the renewal checks compare the request with the client certificate and verify that certificate.
  13. The router calls the CA and encodes its answer or sends its error.

Embedding the server lists the endpoints. Errors lists the status and message of each refusal.

docs.title: Request handling on the client
docs.text:
Each client method:

  1. Picks a proxy from Client.Proxy or the environment and opens a TCP connection, through a CONNECT tunnel when a proxy applies.
  2. Runs the TLS handshake with the trust anchors and client certificate or the TLS-SRP handshake with SRPUsername and SRPPassword. OnConnect then sees the connection.
  3. For Enroll and Reenroll with SigningKey set, signs the CSR again with the tls-unique value of this connection as its challenge password. Only TLS 1.2, including TLS-SRP, has that value. Only an RSA or ECDSA SigningKey can sign the new request.
  4. Sends one request with the Basic or bearer credentials and AdditionalHeaders, through WrapTransport when it is set.
  5. Reads at most MaxResponseBody bytes, returns any status other than 200 as an est.Error and decodes the rest.

The connection is closed when the method returns. The client keeps no state between calls, so one Client value can run any number of operations.

docs.title: What stays with the host
docs.text:
• TLS. The host chooses the server certificate, the TLS versions and which client certificates the handshake accepts.
  • The CA. Signing, certificate profiles, revocation and any approval workflow are behind the CA interface.
  • Who may enroll. Without CheckBasicAuth or CheckBearerToken every enrollment request is accepted.
  • Proof of possession. The router does not check the tls-unique challenge password. A CA that needs the binding checks it.
  • Retries. A CA that answers 202 with a Retry-After value does not get polled. The client returns the status and the value and the caller decides when to try again.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page starts the bundled test server, enrolls a certificate with the command line client and renews it. It then shows the same steps in Go. Everything runs on one machine.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Go 1.27.3 or newer
  • OpenSSL, to print a fingerprint in step 3 and to generate a private key in step 4
  • Port 8443 free on the local machine

docs.title: Step 1: install the tools
docs.text:
go install github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est/cmd/estclient@latest

go install github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est/cmd/estserver@latest

Both land in $(go env GOPATH)/bin or in GOBIN when it is set. That directory must be on your PATH.

docs.title: Step 2: start the server
docs.text:
estserver &

Without a configuration file the server creates a new test CA in memory, a root and an intermediate that live for 24 hours. It listens on localhost:8443 and issues a certificate to anyone who asks, so it is for testing only. Its log goes to standard error. The CA is gone when the server stops. estserver describes the configuration file.

docs.title: Step 3: get the CA certificates
docs.text:
The test CA is new, so nothing trusts it yet. Fetch its root once without checking the server certificate and save it as the explicit trust anchor:

estclient cacerts -server localhost:8443 -insecure -roots -out anchor.pem

-insecure accepts any server, so a real deployment checks the fetched root out of band before it trusts it, for example by comparing its fingerprint with one the CA operator published:

openssl x509 -in anchor.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256

Every later command verifies the server against anchor.pem. Fetch the full CA chain with it, because renewal needs the intermediate in step 6:

estclient cacerts -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -out cacerts.pem

cacerts.pem holds the intermediate and the root.

docs.title: Step 4: enroll with your own key
docs.text:
Generate a key and a certificate signing request (CSR), then enroll:

openssl genrsa -out key.pem 3072

estclient csr -key key.pem -cn 'John Doe' -emails 'john@doe.com' -out csr.pem

estclient enroll -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -csr csr.pem -out cert.pem

enroll can also build the CSR itself from -key and the same name flags as csr, so the csr step is optional. The test CA copies the subject and the subject alternative names from the request and issues a certificate that is valid until its CA expires, at most 24 hours.

docs.title: Step 5: let the server generate the key
docs.text:
estclient serverkeygen -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -cn 'Jane Doe' -out jane.pem -keyout jane-key.pem

The server generates a 2048-bit RSA key and returns it with the certificate. jane-key.pem holds a PRIVATE KEY block and is created readable by its owner only. Without -csr the client signs the request with a temporary key, because the server ignores the key in the request.

docs.title: Step 6: renew
docs.text:
A renewal authenticates with the certificate being renewed in the TLS handshake. The server asks for client certificates issued under its root, so the client must send the intermediate as well. Put the certificate and the CA chain in one file:

cat cert.pem cacerts.pem > certs.pem

estclient reenroll -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -key key.pem -certs certs.pem -out newcert.pem

Without -csr the client builds the request from the subject and the subject alternative names of the first certificate in -certs and signs it with -key. The server refuses a renewal whose request names anything else.

Stop the server when you are done:

kill %1

docs.title: The same from Go
docs.text:
The client is a struct with the server address and the trust anchor. Each method runs one EST operation on its own TLS connection and takes a context, here ctx with a 30-second deadline:

client := &est.Client{
    Host:           host,
    ExplicitAnchor: anchor,
}

cacerts, err := client.CACerts(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("CA:", cacerts[0].Subject.CommonName)

key, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
der, err := x509.CreateCertificateRequest(rand.Reader, &x509.CertificateRequest{
    Subject:  pkix.Name{CommonName: "device-1"},
    DNSNames: []string{"device-1.example.com"},
}, key)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
csr, err := x509.ParseCertificateRequest(der)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cert, err := client.Enroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("enrolled:", cert.Subject.CommonName, cert.DNSNames)

Renewal adds the certificate being renewed and its key to the client, which presents them in the TLS handshake:

// The certificate being renewed authenticates the TLS connection.
client.Certificates = []*x509.Certificate{cert}
client.PrivateKey = key

// The request repeats the Subject and SubjectAltName of the certificate.
der, err = x509.CreateCertificateRequest(rand.Reader, &x509.CertificateRequest{
    RawSubject: cert.RawSubject,
    DNSNames:   cert.DNSNames,
}, key)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
csr, err = x509.ParseCertificateRequest(der)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

renewed, err := client.Reenroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("renewed:", renewed.Subject.CommonName, renewed.SerialNumber.Cmp(cert.SerialNumber) != 0)

This code is the ExampleClient function in example_test.go, which runs it against a test server with go test -run ExampleClient. It prints:

CA: Example EST CA
enrolled: device-1 [device-1.example.com]
renewed: device-1 true

docs.title: Interoperability
docs.text: This page lists only peers that were run against go-pki-est code, with where the evidence lives. The library's own tests run the client against its own router, which proves the two halves agree but not that they follow other implementations.

docs.title: Cisco libest 3.2.0
docs.text: certrally is a command line tool whose est commands are built on est.Client. It always sets AllowCertificateChain. Its tests run against the example server of Cisco libest 3.2.0, built from tag r3.2.0 (commit 4ca02c6d) on Ubuntu 20.04 with OpenSSL 1.1.1. Only the client side of go-pki-est is exercised.

docs.title: Checked in CI
docs.text:
The Cisco libest job of the certrally integration workflow runs on pushes and pull requests to certrally's dev and main branches, weekly and on demand. certrally currently pins go-pki-est v1.4.0. Every request uses a new ECDSA P-256 key, certrally's default. The steps are in libest_test.go.

Client operation Result CACerts with an explicit anchor Works CACerts with InsecureSkipVerify and a fingerprint check Works CSRAttrs Works Enroll with a password Works Reenroll with the client certificate against a server started with -o Works Reenroll with a password and no client certificate Works Enroll over TLS-SRP with a 2048-bit group Works Enroll with SigningKey against a server started with -t Works Enroll without SigningKey against a server started with -t The server answers 401 Proof of Possession Mismatch ServerKeyGen Fails. The server declares a Content-Length shorter than its multipart response, so the client reads unexpected EOF

docs.title: Manual notes
docs.text:
certrally's Tested servers page also records manual runs against the same server. They were written when certrally used go-pki-est v1.3.1 and CI does not repeat them:

  • Enroll worked with ECDSA P-384, RSA 2048 and Ed25519 keys.
  • ML-DSA and composite ML-DSA requests get 400, because OpenSSL 1.1.1 does not know the algorithms.
  • The passwd.srpv file that comes with libest uses a 1536-bit group, which the client refuses by default. Use a verifier with at least 2048 bits or lower SRPMinGroupBits.
  • A server started with -h asks for HTTP Digest authentication. The client signs in with Basic only and gets 401.
  • A server started with -m answers enrollments with 202 and Retry-After: 3600.

docs.title: Accommodations in go-pki-est
docs.text: The router's 401 challenge uses the header name WWW-Authenticate exactly, because libest compares header names with case. The client sends requests with a Content-Length, because the libest server cannot read a chunked body.

docs.title: Not tested
docs.text:
No other EST server or client has been run against go-pki-est with recorded results. This includes the estserver router with libest's client, Bouncy Castle, OpenSSL-based clients and commercial EST servers. The source carries workarounds for Bouncy Castle, such as the 401 challenge without a body, but no test runs Bouncy Castle.

To report a result, open an issue with the peer, its version, the operations you ran and sanitized evidence, as CONTRIBUTING.md asks.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
• No /fullcmc. Full CMC (RFC 7030 section 4.3) is not implemented. A request answers 404.
  • No CMS error responses. RFC 7030 section 4.2.3 allows an enrollment error as a CMC simple PKI response. The router sends errors as plain text and the client reads only plain text, JSON or empty bodies as messages.
  • No HTTP Digest authentication. The client signs in with Basic, a bearer token, a client certificate or TLS-SRP. A server that asks for Digest, such as libest with -h, answers 401.
  • No automatic retry. A 202 answer returns an error with RetryAfter. The caller schedules the retry.
  • Redirects are refused. RFC 7030 allows redirects within the same origin, but the client follows none.

docs.title: Proof of possession
docs.text:
• The router does not check the tls-unique challenge password. The CA compares it with the connection when it wants the binding.
  • TLS 1.3 has no tls-unique value. The client adds no challenge password over TLS 1.3, which includes every renewal with an ML-DSA certificate.

docs.title: Post-quantum algorithms
docs.text:
• Composite ML-DSA and SLH-DSA need CheckCSRSignature and, for client certificates that such a CA signed, VerifyClientCertificate. The library brings no implementation of either.
  • Certificates with composite ML-DSA or SLH-DSA keys cannot renew over TLS. crypto/tls cannot present them. Use password renewal or TLS-SRP.
  • estclient serverkeygen cannot write ML-KEM keys. The library returns them.

See Post-quantum algorithms.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
• No revocation check on renewal. The CA must refuse revoked certificates itself.
  • The rate limit is server-wide. Limits per client belong in a hook.
  • The router must terminate TLS. A proxy that terminates TLS in front of it hides the client certificate.
  • TLS-SRP needs a second listener from go-tls-srp. It runs TLS 1.2 only.

docs.title: Command line tools
docs.text:
• estserver is for testing. Its mock CA issues to anyone, without authentication.
  • estclient has no TLS-SRP options and no options for AllowCertificateChain or MaxResponseBody.
  • estclient cannot read ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY files. Only keys encrypted in the legacy PEM format prompt for a passphrase.
  • estclient tpmenroll is not tested against a TPM. No test activates a credential on a TPM device.

docs.title: Interoperability
docs.text: Only Cisco libest 3.2.0 has been run against the client with recorded results. Its /serverkeygen responses cannot be read, because the server declares a short Content-Length. See Interoperability.

docs.title: Post-quantum algorithms
docs.text:
What works depends on what Go's crypto/x509 and crypto/tls support. Go 1.27 has ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in crypto/mldsa and accepts it in certificates, requests and TLS 1.3. It has no SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) and no composite ML-DSA. The library hands those algorithms to hooks that the host fills with another implementation.

Algorithm Enroll Renew with the certificate over TLS /serverkeygen ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87 Yes Yes, over TLS 1.3 Yes Composite ML-DSA With CheckCSRSignature No, use password renewal or TLS-SRP Yes, as PKCS #8 SLH-DSA With CheckCSRSignature No, use password renewal or TLS-SRP Yes, as PKCS #8 ML-KEM No, it cannot sign a request No Yes, as PKCS #8

The tests and examples use ML-DSA-65. The other rows follow from the code paths described below.

docs.title: ML-DSA
docs.text:
An ML-DSA request enrolls like any other. The renewal presents the ML-DSA certificate, which crypto/tls accepts only in TLS 1.3:

key, err := mldsa.GenerateKey(mldsa.MLDSA65())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
csr, err := newCSR(key, "device-8")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
cert, err := client.Enroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Printf("enrolled: %s with %T\n", cert.Subject.CommonName, cert.PublicKey)

// The ML-DSA certificate authenticates the renewal.
client.Certificates = []*x509.Certificate{cert}
client.PrivateKey = key
client.OnConnect = func(conn net.Conn) {
    fmt.Println("renewing over", tls.VersionName(conn.(*tls.Conn).ConnectionState().Version))
}
renewed, err := client.Reenroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("renewed:", renewed.Subject.CommonName)

ExampleClient_mldsa in example_test.go prints:

enrolled: device-8 with *mldsa.PublicKey
renewing over TLS 1.3
renewed: device-8
  • No tls-unique binding. TLS 1.3 has no tls-unique value, so the client leaves the challenge password out of the request even when SigningKey is set. A server that requires the binding refuses ML-DSA renewals over TLS.
  • The listener must allow TLS 1.3, which crypto/tls does by default.
  • estclient enrolls and renews with an ML-DSA key in a PKCS #8 PEM file given with -key.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
crypto/x509 parses these requests but cannot verify their signatures, so the router answers 400 unsupported PKCS10 certificate signing request signature algorithm by default. Set CheckCSRSignature to verify them with another implementation:

  • Return nil to accept the request. The CA receives it with a nil PublicKey, because crypto/x509 does not know the key type. The CA reads the key from RawSubjectPublicKeyInfo.
  • Return an est.Error to send its status. Any other error answers 400 invalid PKCS10 certificate signing request signature.

/serverkeygen never calls the hook, because RFC 7030 section 4.4.1 tells the server to ignore the request signature.

Go cannot sign these requests. Build them with another library and parse them with x509.ParseCertificateRequest. est.Client sends the bytes of the parsed request as they are.

docs.title: Request size
docs.text: An SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f signature alone is 49,856 bytes, so the request takes about 67 KB in base64. That is over the 64 KiB default of MaxRequestBody. Raise it and raise the client's MaxResponseBody when the CA chain uses such certificates. See Refusals and limits.

docs.title: Renewal
docs.text: TLS has no signature scheme that crypto/tls offers for composite ML-DSA or SLH-DSA keys, so a client cannot present such a certificate in the handshake. Renew these certificates with password renewal or TLS-SRP.

docs.title: Certificates that a post-quantum CA signed
docs.text:
A client certificate with a classical or ML-DSA key may be signed by an SLH-DSA or composite ML-DSA CA. crypto/x509 cannot verify that signature, so the built-in renewal check refuses it. Set VerifyClientCertificate to check the certificate with another implementation and configure the listener with ClientAuth: tls.RequestClientCert. With VerifyClientCertIfGiven or RequireAndVerifyClientCert, crypto/tls refuses the certificate before the router sees it.

The router still compares the request with the certificate before it calls the hook. See Custom certificate verification.

docs.title: ML-KEM
docs.text:
ML-KEM keys encrypt and cannot sign a request, so they come only from /serverkeygen. The router recognizes PKCS #8 by its structure and sends keys that crypto/x509 cannot parse, such as ML-KEM, as they are. Client.ServerKeyGen returns the key bytes without parsing them.

estclient serverkeygen writes only keys that crypto/x509 parses or encrypted PKCS #7 keys and fails with unrecognized private key format for an ML-KEM key.

docs.title: Key exchange
docs.text: The hybrid key exchanges X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 are part of the TLS 1.3 defaults of crypto/tls. est.Client uses those defaults. A server that leaves CurvePreferences unset offers them too. estserver limits its curves to P-521, P-384 and P-256, so it does not use them.

docs.title: Encoding and transport
docs.text: Behavior Coverage Base64 bodies (section 4) Sent wrapped at 76 characters. Spaces, tabs and line breaks are accepted on receipt, as RFC 8951 section 3.1 asks Content-Transfer-Encoding (RFC 8951) Ignored on receipt. The server sends it unless OmitTransferEncoding is set Retry-After (section 4.2.3) The client returns it with the status as Error.RetryAfter, from seconds or an HTTP date. It does not wait or retry Redirects (section 3.2.1) The client returns a 3xx as an error and never follows it HTTP proxies The client tunnels through http and https proxies with CONNECT TLS versions The client accepts TLS 1.2 and 1.3. TLS-SRP runs over TLS 1.2 only

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: CI builds and tests the module on Linux and macOS and builds it on Windows. The Linux job also runs the estclient tests that sign with a SoftHSM key. No CI job has a TPM, so the TPM tests of estclient are skipped everywhere.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text: EST servers identify clients by a TLS client certificate, an HTTP credential or a TLS-SRP password. The client sends whatever its fields name on every request, including /cacerts and /csrattrs. Which ones a server requires is up to the server.

docs.title: Client certificates and hardware keys
docs.text:
Set Certificates and PrivateKey to present a certificate in the TLS handshake. The client presents it only when both are set.

  • Certificates holds the client certificate first, followed by the intermediates the server needs. The root may be left out.
  • PrivateKey may be any crypto.Signer, so the key can stay in a hardware security module or a TPM. estclient uses this for its HSM and TPM keys.

The client presents it when the server asks for a certificate, as long as the server names no CAs or one of the certificates in Certificates was issued by a CA it names. Otherwise it sends none. For Reenroll it must be the certificate being renewed, see Renewing a certificate.

docs.title: HTTP Basic
docs.text: Username and Password are sent as HTTP Basic credentials (RFC 7030 section 3.2.3) when Username is not empty. They suit a first enrollment, before the device holds a certificate. The client offers only Basic. A server that asks for HTTP Digest answers 401.

docs.title: Bearer tokens
docs.text:
BearerToken is sent as Authorization: Bearer <token> (RFC 6750). Basic credentials take precedence: with Username set, the token is not sent. A go-pki-est server checks the token only when it sets CheckBearerToken. Without that hook the token signs nothing in.

The header goes to the EST server only. A proxy gets its own credentials from the proxy URL, see Connections and hooks.

docs.title: Extra headers
docs.text: AdditionalHeaders adds HTTP headers to every request, for servers that read settings from them. estserver, for example, reads the key size of /serverkeygen from Bit-Size. HostHeader replaces the Host header, which is mostly useful for tests.

docs.title: TLS-SRP
docs.text:
TLS-SRP (RFC 5054) signs in with a username and password during the TLS handshake, as RFC 7030 section 3.3.3 allows. The password also authenticates the server, so the client needs no trust anchor:

client := &est.Client{
    Host:        ln.Addr().String(),
    SRPUsername: "device-5",
    SRPPassword: "srp-secret",
}

cert, err := client.Enroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("enrolled:", cert.Subject.CommonName)

// The password signs the client in, so no client certificate is needed.
renewed, err := client.Reenroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("renewed:", renewed.Subject.CommonName)
  • ExplicitAnchor, ImplicitAnchor, InsecureSkipVerify and Certificates are not used.
  • TLS-SRP runs over TLS 1.2 with AES-CBC cipher suites. The tls-unique binding of SigningKey therefore works.
  • The client refuses SRP groups smaller than SRPMinGroupBits, 2048 bits by default. libest ships an example verifier file with a 1536-bit group, which fails with srptls: server chose the 1536 bit SRP group, below the minimum of 2048 bits.
  • A wrong password fails the handshake with an error that wraps srptls.ErrWrongPassword. An unknown username fails with srptls.ErrUnknownUsername, unless the server hides which usernames exist. Both errors come from go-tls-srp.
  • OnConnect receives a *srptls.Conn instead of a *tls.Conn.

docs.title: Renewal without the certificate
docs.text:
RFC 7030 section 2.3 allows a renewal that a password signs in instead of the certificate being renewed. Leave Certificates empty and set the credential:

client.Username = "device-3"
client.Password = "renewal-secret"

csr, err := newCSR(key, "device-3")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
renewed, err := client.Reenroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("renewed without a client certificate:", renewed.Subject.CommonName)

// The CA refuses a request that names another subject.
other, err := newCSR(key, "device-4")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
_, err = client.Reenroll(ctx, other)
fmt.Println(strings.TrimSpace(err.Error()))

A go-pki-est server accepts this only with ServerConfig.PasswordRenewal set or over TLS-SRP. The CA then decides which certificate is renewed and refuses a request for an identity the user does not own, as the example shows. Use this for certificates that cannot authenticate TLS, such as composite ML-DSA certificates.

docs.title: Connections and hooks
docs.text: How the client reaches the server, what it accepts in a response and how a program can watch it.

docs.title: Proxies
docs.text:
Proxy chooses the proxy, like http.Transport.Proxy. When it is nil, http.ProxyFromEnvironment applies, so HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY decide. It never proxies localhost or a loopback address. A function that returns nil connects directly.

proxyURL, err := url.Parse("http://proxy-user:proxy-secret@proxy.example.com:3128")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
client := &est.Client{
    Host:        "est.example.com:8443",
    Proxy:       http.ProxyURL(proxyURL),
    BearerToken: "token-from-the-identity-provider",
}
  • The client opens a CONNECT tunnel through the proxy and runs TLS or TLS-SRP to the EST server inside it. The proxy never sees the EST requests and OnConnect and the tls-unique binding work as on a direct connection.
  • http and https proxies are supported. An https proxy is checked against the system roots. Any other scheme fails with unsupported proxy scheme "socks5", want http or https.
  • The user and password in the proxy URL are sent as Basic Proxy-Authorization.
  • A proxy that answers the CONNECT with anything but 200 fails the call with proxy <proxy> refused the tunnel to <server>: <status>.

docs.title: Watching the connection and the requests
docs.text:
OnConnect receives the connection of each operation after the handshake and before the request. WrapTransport wraps the HTTP transport, so it sees every request and response:

client.OnConnect = func(conn net.Conn) {
    if c, ok := conn.(*tls.Conn); ok {
        fmt.Println("connected with", tls.VersionName(c.ConnectionState().Version))
    }
}
client.WrapTransport = func(next http.RoundTripper) http.RoundTripper {
    return roundTripFunc(func(r *http.Request) (*http.Response, error) {
        resp, err := next.RoundTrip(r)
        if err == nil {
            fmt.Println(r.Method, r.URL.Path, resp.Status)
        }
        return resp, err
    })
}

ExampleClient_hooks in example_test.go prints:

connected with TLS 1.3
GET /.well-known/est/cacerts 200 OK
  • OnConnect receives a *tls.Conn or a *srptls.Conn with TLS-SRP. It must not read from, write to or close the connection.
  • The wrapper must pass every request on to the transport it wraps. That transport already applies MaxResponseBody, so the wrapper sees bounded bodies.

docs.title: Response limits
docs.text:
The client reads at most MaxResponseBody bytes of a response body, 1 MiB by default. The limit covers error messages and all parts of a multipart response. A larger body fails the call with an error that contains response body larger than 1048576 bytes.

Raise the limit when responses carry large post-quantum certificates. An SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f signature alone is 49,856 bytes, so each certificate signed with it takes about 67 KB in base64. A negative value fails every call with MaxResponseBody must not be negative.

docs.title: Accepting a chain in the response
docs.text: RFC 7030 section 4.2.3 allows only the issued certificate in an enrollment response. When a server adds its CA certificates, Enroll, Reenroll and ServerKeyGen fail with <n> certificates returned. Set AllowCertificateChain to accept such a response. The client then returns the one certificate that issued none of the others, matched by name. A response in which that is not exactly one certificate still fails.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text: The client never follows a redirect. A 3xx answer returns an est.Error with that status. RFC 7030 section 3.2.1 allows only redirects within the same origin and following one would send the credentials to another location.

docs.title: Timeouts and connection reuse
docs.text:
Each call takes a context, which bounds the proxy tunnel, the handshake and the request. The client has no timeout of its own, so pass a context with a deadline.

Every call uses a new connection and closes it when it returns. DisableKeepAlives also sends Connection: close with each request.

docs.title: Enrollment and renewal
docs.text: est.Client runs one EST operation per method call. Each call opens its own connection, runs the TLS handshake, sends one request and closes the connection. The context of the call bounds all of it.

docs.title: Creating a client
docs.text:
Only Host is required. It is the host:port of the server, such as est.example.com:8443, without a scheme or path. The listing in the next section creates a client.

  • AdditionalPathSegment selects one of several CAs that the server offers (RFC 7030 section 3.2.2). The client then calls https://<host>/.well-known/est/<segment>/<operation>.
  • Trust anchors authenticate the server. ExplicitAnchor is used when it is set. Otherwise ImplicitAnchor is used. When neither is set, the system roots apply.
  • InsecureSkipVerify accepts any server certificate. Use it only to fetch the CA certificates once and check them out of band, as Getting started does. Every later call needs a trust anchor.

Signing in adds credentials and Connections and hooks covers proxies, limits and tracing. Client fields lists every field.

docs.title: Getting the CA certificates
docs.text:
CACerts returns every certificate of the /cacerts response in the order the server sent them. In this listing and the ones below, ctx is a context with a deadline, such as one from context.WithTimeout:

client := &est.Client{
    Host:           host,
    ExplicitAnchor: anchor,
}

cacerts, err := client.CACerts(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("CA:", cacerts[0].Subject.CommonName)

key, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
der, err := x509.CreateCertificateRequest(rand.Reader, &x509.CertificateRequest{
    Subject:  pkix.Name{CommonName: "device-1"},
    DNSNames: []string{"device-1.example.com"},
}, key)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
csr, err := x509.ParseCertificateRequest(der)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cert, err := client.Enroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("enrolled:", cert.Subject.CommonName, cert.DNSNames)

The same listing shows Enroll. It sends a PKCS #10 request, usually created with x509.CreateCertificateRequest and returns the issued certificate.

RFC 7030 section 4.2.3 allows only the issued certificate in the response. Some servers add the CA chain. The client refuses such a response unless AllowCertificateChain is set, see Connections and hooks.

docs.title: Binding the request to the TLS session
docs.text:
RFC 7030 section 3.5 lets the client put the tls-unique value of the TLS session into the challenge password of the CSR, which proves that the requester holds the key on this connection. Set SigningKey to the key that signs the CSR. The client then signs the request again with the challenge password added, in Enroll and Reenroll.

  • SigningKey must be an RSA or ECDSA key. Over TLS 1.2 another key, such as Ed25519 or ML-DSA, fails the call with x509: only RSA and ECDSA keys supported.
  • tls-unique exists only in TLS 1.2. Over TLS 1.3 the client sends the request unchanged. TLS-SRP always runs over TLS 1.2, so the binding works there.
  • The client has no setting to cap the TLS version. Against a server that offers TLS 1.3 the binding is never added.
  • The router does not check the challenge password. A CA that requires the binding must compare it with the session itself.

docs.title: Renewing a certificate
docs.text:
Reenroll renews a certificate. The certificate being renewed authenticates the TLS connection, so set Certificates and PrivateKey:

// The certificate being renewed authenticates the TLS connection.
client.Certificates = []*x509.Certificate{cert}
client.PrivateKey = key

// The request repeats the Subject and SubjectAltName of the certificate.
der, err = x509.CreateCertificateRequest(rand.Reader, &x509.CertificateRequest{
    RawSubject: cert.RawSubject,
    DNSNames:   cert.DNSNames,
}, key)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
csr, err = x509.ParseCertificateRequest(der)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

renewed, err := client.Reenroll(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println("renewed:", renewed.Subject.CommonName, renewed.SerialNumber.Cmp(cert.SerialNumber) != 0)
  • The request must repeat the Subject and the SubjectAltName extension of the certificate, byte for byte, as RFC 7030 section 4.2.2 requires. A go-pki-est server refuses any difference with 403. Building the request from RawSubject and the names of the certificate keeps both equal. A new key is allowed, so the same call rekeys.
  • Send the intermediates. Certificates holds the client certificate first and the CA certificates the server needs to build the chain after it. When the server names the CAs it accepts, the Go TLS client presents the certificate only if one of the certificates in the list was issued by one of them. Otherwise it sends no certificate. estserver names only its root, so without the intermediate the client presents nothing and the server answers 403 client certificate must be provided for /simplereenroll.
  • Servers may also accept a renewal signed in with a password, a bearer token or TLS-SRP instead of the certificate. See Signing in.

docs.title: Server-generated keys
docs.text:
ServerKeyGen asks the server to generate the key (RFC 7030 section 4.4). The server ignores the key and the signature of the request and uses only its names, so a throwaway key may sign it:

// The request carries the names. The server ignores its key, so a throwaway key signs it.
throwaway, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
csr, err := newCSR(throwaway, "device-2")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cert, keyDER, err := client.ServerKeyGen(ctx, csr)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
// Without additional encryption the key is PKCS #8.
key, err := x509.ParsePKCS8PrivateKey(keyDER)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Printf("certificate: %s\nkey: %T\n", cert.Subject.CommonName, key)

The key comes back as DER bytes in one of two forms:

  • PKCS #8 in an application/pkcs8 part, when the server adds no encryption. Parse it with x509.ParsePKCS8PrivateKey. Keys that crypto/x509 does not know, such as ML-KEM, are returned as they are.
  • CMS in an application/pkcs7-mime; smime-type=server-generated-key part, when the server encrypts the key. The client returns the CMS bytes without decrypting them. Decrypt them with the key or password your CA agreed with the client.

The response must hold exactly two parts, a key and a certificate. Otherwise ServerKeyGen fails with no certificate returned, no private key returned or more than 2 parts in HTTP response.

docs.title: CSR attributes
docs.text:
CSRAttrs returns the attributes the CA wants in a request (RFC 7030 section 4.5):

attrs, err := client.CSRAttrs(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, oid := range attrs.OIDs {
    fmt.Println("OID:", oid)
}
for _, attr := range attrs.Attributes {
    fmt.Println("attribute:", attr.Type, attr.Values)
}

OIDs holds the bare object identifiers and Attributes the attributes with values. Values of type OBJECT IDENTIFIER, BOOLEAN, INTEGER and most string types become asn1.ObjectIdentifier, bool, *big.Int and string. Other values stay asn1.RawValue. A 204 or 404 answer means the server has no attributes to ask for, so CSRAttrs returns an empty value and no error.

docs.title: Deferred and refused requests
docs.text:
Every status other than 200 returns an error that implements est.Error, including 202 Accepted, because a deferred enrollment has no certificate yet:

_, err = client.Enroll(ctx, csr)
if estErr, ok := errors.AsType[est.Error](err); ok {
    fmt.Println("status:", estErr.StatusCode())
    fmt.Println("retry after:", estErr.RetryAfter())
    fmt.Println("message:", strings.TrimSpace(estErr.Error()))
}

RetryAfter comes from the Retry-After header, given in seconds or as an HTTP date and is 0 without one. The client never retries or polls. Repeat the same call after the delay to collect the certificate. Error() returns the response body, which a go-pki-est server writes as the status and the reason followed by a newline. Errors lists them.

Errors without an HTTP status, such as a failed handshake, a refused proxy tunnel, an expired context or a response that does not decode, do not implement est.Error.

docs.title: TPM enrollment
docs.text:
/tpmenroll is an operation outside RFC 7030 that came with globalsign/est. It issues a certificate for a key on a TPM 2.0 device and returns it so that only the TPM that holds the key and the endorsement key (EK) can read it. It uses the credential protection of the TPM 2.0 Library specification: the CA encrypts a secret to the EK, bound to the name of the key being certified and the TPM releases the secret only to TPM2_ActivateCredential.

Because it is not part of RFC 7030, use it with a go-pki-est server whose CA implements TPMEnroll.

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
Client.TPMEnroll takes these arguments after the context:

Argument Content csr The certificate request. It is sent like an enrollment request and its signature is checked ekCerts The EK certificate first, then its chain. At least one certificate ekPub The public area of the EK in TPM encoding akPub The public area of the key being certified in TPM encoding

The server checks that the public key in ekPub matches the EK certificate and answers 422 public key in public area doesn't match when it does not. The credential is bound to the key that akPub describes, so only a TPM that holds that key and the EK can read the certificate. The server does not compare akPub with the key in the CSR. A CA that needs them to match compares them itself.

docs.title: The response
docs.text:
TPMEnroll returns three byte slices:

Value Content credBlob The encrypted credential, for TPM2_ActivateCredential encSeed The seed encrypted to the EK, for TPM2_ActivateCredential cred A CMS EnvelopedData that holds the certificate, encrypted with the credential as a pre-shared key

The client returns the three values as they are. The caller loads the key and the EK on the TPM, runs TPM2_ActivateCredential to recover the credential and decrypts cred with it. estclient tpmenroll does all of this, see estclient.

docs.title: The CA side
docs.text:
CA.TPMEnroll receives the parsed request, the EK certificates and both public areas and returns the three values. The mock CA behind estserver issues the certificate as for /simpleenroll, generates a 16-byte AES key as the credential and encrypts the certificate with it. It builds the credential with the module's internal/tpm package, which other modules cannot import.

A CA that does not offer TPM enrollment returns an est.Error with a status such as 501, as the example CA in The CA interface does.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: The library tests run /tpmenroll against the mock CA without a TPM and decrypt the credential in software with the endorsement key. No test activates a credential on a TPM or runs estclient tpmenroll against one.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
You need Go at the version in go.mod, 1.27.3 or newer. The HSM tests also need SoftHSM 2 and the TPM tests a TPM 2.0 device. Without them, skip those tests as Testing shows.

git clone https://github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est.git
cd go-pki-est
GLOBALSIGN_EST_SKIP=hsm,tpm make test

Open pull requests against dev. make help lists every target.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path Content *.go at the root The est package: client, router, CA interface, encoding and errors example_test.go The examples that the documentation site includes cmd/estclient The command line client cmd/estserver The test server and its TLS-SRP listener internal/mockca The mock CA behind estserver internal/tpm The TPM credential protection for /tpmenroll internal/basiclogger The logger of estserver docs and mkdocs.yml This site

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Run these before submitting a change:

make fmt-check
make lint
GLOBALSIGN_EST_SKIP=hsm,tpm make test
Target Check make fmt-check Every tracked Go file is gofmt formatted make vet go vet ./... make test go vet and the tests under the race detector make lint golangci-lint at the version CI uses, installed under bin/ make lint-config The golangci-lint configuration is valid make tidy-check go.mod and go.sum are tidy. Run it when they change make govulncheck Known vulnerabilities that reach the module. Run it when a dependency changes make actionlint The GitHub Actions workflows. Run it when a workflow changes make gitleaks Credentials in the working tree and the history make docs-build The documentation site, with warnings as errors

Protocol changes need negative tests and an RFC citation. User-facing changes update the Go doc comments, this site and CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Documentation site
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme. The toolchain is pinned with hashes in docs/requirements.txt. Install it in a virtual environment and point PYTHON at it:

make docs-deps PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
make docs-serve PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
  • Go code on the pages comes from example_test.go through snippet sections marked with those with an // Output: comment, so the code on the site cannot drift from the library. Write new Go listings there, not in the Markdown.
  • make docs-build runs with --strict, so a broken link, a missing anchor or a page absent from the navigation fails the build.
  • To change a toolchain version, edit docs/requirements.in and run make docs-requirements, which needs pip-tools.

The documentation workflow runs the same build on every change to the site sources and publishes the site from main.

docs.title: Release process
docs.text: A release starts when a version tag reachable from main is pushed. CHANGELOG.md has one section per version and that section becomes the release description.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
The module uses semantic versioning, see Compatibility. Three places carry the version and must agree:

  • estVersion in client.go, with the v, which the client User-Agent and the server Server header report
  • versionString in cmd/estclient/flags.go and cmd/estserver/flags.go, without the v

The tests fail when the tools and the library report different versions.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. On dev, complete the ## [X.Y.Z] - <date> section in CHANGELOG.md and set the versions.

  2. Merge dev into main and run the release check there:

    GLOBALSIGN_EST_SKIP=hsm,tpm VERSION=v1.4.1 make release-check

    It exports HEAD with git archive, verifies, builds, vets and tests the export and imports it from a separate module, so it catches files that are untracked or only present locally. With VERSION it also checks that CHANGELOG.md has a dated heading for the version and no unreleased section and that estVersion matches.

  3. Create a signed tag and push main and the tag:

    git tag -s v1.4.1 -m 'v1.4.1'
git push origin main v1.4.1

  4. The release workflow repeats the check on the tag, builds the source archives, the SBOM and the checksums, attests their provenance and creates a draft release with the changelog section as its description. Review the draft and publish it.

Do not publish a release in the GitHub web interface. Publishing creates the tag, which starts the workflow. The workflow then refuses to rebuild a release that is already published. A draft that already exists for the tag is updated and gets the artifacts. Push only the new tag. Clones made from globalsign/est hold its v1.0.x tags, which declare the old module path.

Verifying a release shows how users check the artifacts.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
GLOBALSIGN_EST_SKIP=hsm,tpm make test

make test runs go vet and then go test -race -count=1 ./.... TESTFLAGS=-v lists every test, including the skipped ones.

docs.title: What the tests cover
docs.text:
• The root package runs the client against the router in the same process. The tests cover every operation, the renewal checks, the hooks and their combinations, refusals, the limits, TLS-SRP, proxies, bearer tokens, redirects, response limits and ML-DSA.
  • The examples in example_test.go compile with the tests. Those with an // Output: comment also run and compare their output. They are also the Go listings on this site.
  • cmd/estclient runs the commands against an in-process router with the mock CA, including ML-DSA keys, output file permissions and proxies.
  • cmd/estserver tests the default listen address, the timeouts, the TLS-SRP verifier file reader and the TLS-SRP listener.

docs.title: HSM and TPM tests
docs.text:
GLOBALSIGN_EST_SKIP takes a comma-separated list:

  • hsm skips the tests that use a key on SoftHSM.
  • tpm skips the test that needs a TPM 2.0 device.

The HSM tests load the key that cmd/estclient/testdata/test_hsm.cfg names and sign a request with it. In CI the Linux job installs softhsm2 and runs .github/scripts/setup-softhsm.sh, which creates the token Testing Token with PIN 1234, imports an RSA key and rewrites test_hsm.cfg with the library path of the runner. The script writes to the GitHub Actions environment and overwrites the tracked test_hsm.cfg, so do not run it locally. Skip hsm unless you have prepared a matching token yourself.

The only TPM test, TestNewConfigHardware/TPM, loads a TPM key from cmd/estclient/testdata/test_tpm.cfg.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Job Runs Linux make tidy-check, make fmt-check, the build and make test with SoftHSM, skipping tpm macOS The build and make test, skipping hsm and tpm Windows The build only Lint make lint-config, make lint and make actionlint Supply chain make govulncheck, make gitleaks and the SBOM Documentation make docs-build

No CI job has a TPM, so the TPM test does not run in CI. No test runs estclient tpmenroll against a TPM. The library tests run /tpmenroll against the mock CA and decrypt the credential in software.

Interoperability with other EST implementations is tested outside this repository, see Interoperability.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Each entry starts with a message as estclient or the library reports it. The library returns the same text without the estclient: prefix and the command context, such as failed to get certificate:.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority

The client does not trust the server certificate. Give the root that issued it with -explicit or ExplicitAnchor. For a new server, fetch the roots once with -insecure, check their fingerprint out of band and use them from then on, see Bootstrapping. estserver without a configuration creates a new CA on every start, so an old anchor stops working after a restart.

dial tcp [::1]:8443: connect: connection refused

Nothing listens at the address. estserver listens on localhost:8443 by default and only there. To serve other hosts, add a tls section with your own certificates, private_key and client_cas and set its listen_address.

failed to make EST client: EST server not specified

-server is missing on the command line and in the configuration file.

proxy <proxy> refused the tunnel to <server>: 407 Proxy Authentication Required

The proxy wants credentials. Put them in the proxy URL, such as http://user:password@proxy.example.com:3128. Other statuses come from the proxy's own policy.

unsupported proxy scheme "socks5", want http or https

Only http and https proxies are supported. Check HTTPS_PROXY when -proxy is not set.

docs.title: Renewing
docs.text:
403 client certificate must be provided for /simplereenroll

The server received no client certificate. Check that -certs or Certificates holds the certificate and its intermediates. Go clients present a certificate only when its chain reaches a CA that the server names in the handshake, which is usually the root. With the certificate alone the client sends nothing. A TLS-SRP client or password renewal avoids the certificate.

remote error: tls: unknown certificate authority

The server refused the client certificate in the handshake. net/http logs an http: TLS handshake error with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority to the ErrorLog of the http.Server, standard error by default. In estserver this line goes to standard error even when log_file is set. The listener's ClientCAs does not contain the root of the client certificate. In estserver a tls section needs client_cas for renewals to work.

403 Subject and SubjectAltName fields in CSR must be identical to certificate being renewed

The request names something else than the certificate being renewed. Leave out -csr so estclient copies the names from the certificate or build the request from cert.RawSubject and the certificate's SubjectAltName extension.

403 invalid client certificate

The certificate does not verify against the roots and intermediates CA.CACerts returns, at the current time, for client authentication. Check that CACerts includes the root, that the certificate has not expired and that it allows client authentication. The router keeps the CACerts result for 5 minutes, so a new root takes effect only once the cached entry is that old. A /cacerts request does not refresh an entry younger than 5 minutes.

docs.title: Enrolling
docs.text:
no private key provided

estclient enroll without -csr needs -key or a key in the configuration file to sign the generated request.

Unauthorized

A hook refused the credentials. The router sends no body, so the client reports the status text. Check -user and -pass or -token. A bearer token counts only when the server sets CheckBearerToken.

202 ... with a Retry-After value

The CA deferred the request. Send the same request again after the given number of seconds. The library returns the value as RetryAfter(). estclient does not print it.

415 Content-Type must be application/pkcs10

A client other than est.Client sent the request with another content type. EST requests are base64 DER with Content-Type: application/pkcs10.

413 request body too large

The request is over MaxRequestBody, 64 KiB by default. Large post-quantum requests, such as SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f, need a higher value.

400 unsupported PKCS10 certificate signing request signature algorithm

crypto/x509 cannot verify the signature, for example of a composite ML-DSA or SLH-DSA request. Set CheckCSRSignature, see Post-quantum algorithms.

2 certificates returned

The server returned the CA chain with the certificate. Set AllowCertificateChain on the client.

response body larger than 1048576 bytes

A response is over MaxResponseBody, 1 MiB by default. Raise it for large post-quantum chains.

unrecognized private key format from estclient serverkeygen

The server returned a key that crypto/x509 cannot parse, such as ML-KEM. Use the library, whose ServerKeyGen returns the bytes as they are.

docs.title: TLS-SRP
docs.text:
srptls: server chose the 1536 bit SRP group, below the minimum of 2048 bits

The verifier uses a small group. Create it again with -gn 2048 or larger or lower SRPMinGroupBits if you accept the weaker group. The server logs remote error: tls: insufficient security level.

srptls: unknown SRP username

The server does not know the user and tells the client so. A server with unknown_user_seed or one that returns SimulatedVerifier, answers like a wrong password instead.

srptls: wrong SRP password

The password does not match the verifier or the user is unknown and the server hides it.

docs.title: Server side
docs.text:
500 internal server error

The CA returned an error that is not an est.Error or panicked. The server log has the cause. Return an est.Error from the CA to send a meaningful status.

400 host not allowed

The Host header names a host that AllowedHosts does not list. Names compare without the port.

429 rate limit exceeded

The server-wide RateLimit is used up. Retry after the Retry-After value, 1 second.

/healthcheck answers 401

The health check always needs a hook to accept the request. In estserver send the Basic user healthcheck with the configured password, such as curl -u healthcheck:xyzzy.

docs.title: Client
docs.text: est.Client runs EST operations against one server. Every field is optional except Host. A client may be reused and each call opens its own connection. The package documentation on pkg.go.dev has the full comments.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Operation Returns CACerts(ctx) GET /cacerts The CA certificates in the order the server sent them CSRAttrs(ctx) GET /csrattrs The attributes, with OIDs and attributes listed separately Enroll(ctx, csr) POST /simpleenroll The issued certificate Reenroll(ctx, csr) POST /simplereenroll The renewed certificate ServerKeyGen(ctx, csr) POST /serverkeygen The certificate and the key bytes, PKCS #8 or CMS TPMEnroll(ctx, csr, ekCerts, ekPub, akPub) POST /tpmenroll The encrypted credential, the encrypted seed and the encrypted certificate

Each method sends the request as given in csr.Raw, except that SigningKey may add a challenge password. An answer other than 200 returns an est.Error, see Errors.

A nil URL connects directly DisableKeepAlives false Sends Connection: close with every request AllowCertificateChain false Accept an enrollment response that also carries CA certificates MaxResponseBody 1 MiB Largest response body. A negative value fails every call WrapTransport None Wraps the HTTP transport, for example to trace requests OnConnect None Receives the connection after the handshake

docs.title: Fixed behavior
docs.text:
• The TLS connection uses the crypto/tls defaults, which require TLS 1.2 or newer.
  • The client never follows redirects.
  • It sends User-Agent: go-pki-est EST client v1.4.0 github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est, with the library version.
  • It has no timeout of its own. The context of each call bounds the proxy tunnel, the handshake and the request.

docs.title: CSR attributes
docs.text: CSRAttrs holds two lists. OIDs has the bare object identifiers. Attributes has the attributes, each with a Type and Values. Values of type OBJECT IDENTIFIER, BOOLEAN, INTEGER and most string types are decoded into asn1.ObjectIdentifier, bool, *big.Int and string. Other values stay asn1.RawValue. Marshal and Unmarshal convert to and from the DER of RFC 7030 section 4.5.2, which a CA uses to answer /csrattrs.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
The module uses semantic versioning. The library API is the exported identifiers of the root package est. Other modules cannot import the packages under internal. Changes to the options and configuration fields of estclient and estserver are recorded in the changelog too.

CHANGELOG.md has one section per version and describes every change that affects callers, including any that needs a code change.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• Structs gain fields in minor releases, as MaxRequestBody did in 1.2.0. Construct Client, ServerConfig and Refusal with field names.
  • Read the changelog sections between your version and the new one before upgrading. A change that a peer can observe, such as a new status code or header, is listed there.

docs.title: Go version
docs.text: go.mod declares the minimum Go version, currently 1.27.3. CI builds and tests with the version in go.mod. Go 1.27.3 fixes GO-2026-6809 in crypto/x509, which the server reaches when it verifies client certificates.

docs.title: Moving from globalsign/est
docs.text:
go-pki-est continues globalsign/est v1.0.7 under a new module path. Its versions continue from v1.0.7, so v1.1.0 is the first release here.

  1. Replace the import path github.com/globalsign/est with github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est. The package name stays est.
  2. Read the changelog sections from 1.1.0 on. The changes that affect existing code:
    • Go 1.27.3 or newer is required. globalsign/est v1.0.7 declared Go 1.23.0.
    • X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For are ignored unless TrustProxyHeaders is set. True-Client-IP stays ignored, as in v1.0.7.
    • A 405 answer carries an Allow header that lists the supported methods.
    • CheckBasicAuth runs for every enrollment request, also one without credentials, so a hook that treated empty credentials as a mistake must accept or refuse them on purpose.
    • The User-Agent and Server headers name go-pki-est.
    • Renewals no longer fall back to the system roots when they verify client certificates.
    • The client refuses redirects and bounds response bodies.
  3. estserver listens on localhost:8443 by default. Set tls.listen_address to serve other hosts.

Clones of globalsign/est carry its v1.0.x tags, which declare the old module path. go get cannot fetch those tags under the new path.

docs.title: The est.Error interface
docs.text:
type Error interface {
    StatusCode() int
    Error() string
    RetryAfter() int
}

Both sides use it. A CA or a hook returns an est.Error to choose the HTTP status, the message and the Retry-After value. The client returns one for every answer other than 200.

docs.title: Errors the client returns
docs.text:
Error Cause An est.Error The server answered with another status than 200. 202 is included, so a deferred enrollment is an error with RetryAfter set A dial or handshake error, such as dial tcp [::1]:8443: connect: connection refused or tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority The connection, the proxy tunnel or the handshake failed. These errors are returned without a common prefix failed to execute HTTP request: ... Sending the request or reading the response failed after the handshake, for example when a TLS 1.3 server refuses the client certificate, which the client learns only after its handshake <n> certificates returned An enrollment response carried more than one certificate and AllowCertificateChain is not set <n> certificates returned and <m> of them issued no other AllowCertificateChain is set, but the response does not hold exactly one certificate that issued none of the others no certificate returned An enrollment response carried no certificate response body larger than <n> bytes A response went over MaxResponseBody MaxResponseBody must not be negative The client is misconfigured unsupported proxy scheme "<scheme>", want http or https Proxy returned a URL with another scheme proxy <proxy> refused the tunnel to <server>: <status> The proxy answered the CONNECT with another status than 200 srptls: ... A TLS-SRP handshake failed, see Signing in

Read the status of an est.Error with errors.AsType:

_, err = client.Enroll(ctx, csr)
if estErr, ok := errors.AsType[est.Error](err); ok {
    fmt.Println("status:", estErr.StatusCode())
    fmt.Println("retry after:", estErr.RetryAfter())
    fmt.Println("message:", strings.TrimSpace(estErr.Error()))
}

ExampleError in example_test.go prints:

status: 202
retry after: 600
message: 202 waiting for approval

docs.title: The message of an est.Error
docs.text:
• A text/plain, JSON or problem JSON body becomes the message as sent. So does a body without a content type. The router sends <status> <reason> and a newline, so the message starts with the status. Trim the newline before printing it.
  • An empty body gives the status text, such as Unauthorized for a refused sign-in.
  • A body of another type gives the status text and the type, such as Bad Request (application/octet-stream).
  • Control characters other than newline and tab are escaped, such as \x1b, so a server cannot send terminal escape sequences.

RetryAfter returns the Retry-After header in seconds. An HTTP date is converted to the seconds until that time. A missing, invalid or past value gives 0.

docs.title: Errors the server sends
docs.text:
Most error responses are text/plain; charset=utf-8 with the body <status> <reason> and a newline. A 401 carries no body. A 405 has an empty body. An unknown path answers 404 with the body 404 page not found.

Source Status and body The router's own checks See Refusals and limits CheckBasicAuth or CheckBearerToken returns an est.Error Its status, message and Retry-After, unless the status is 401 CheckBasicAuth or CheckBearerToken returns another error or an est.Error with 401 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge and no body CheckCSRSignature or VerifyClientCertificate returns an est.Error Its status, message and Retry-After CheckCSRSignature returns another error 400 invalid PKCS10 certificate signing request signature. An error that wraps x509.ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm gives 400 unsupported PKCS10 certificate signing request signature algorithm VerifyClientCertificate returns another error 403 invalid client certificate The CA returns an est.Error Its status, message and Retry-After The CA returns another error or panics 500 internal server error. The cause is logged, not sent CACerts fails during the renewal check The CA error, answered as above An unknown path 404 404 page not found A known path with the wrong method 405 with an Allow header and an empty body

A 500 from an est.Error is logged as well.
