docs.title: Fixed limits
docs.text:
• An additional path segment is at most 255 bytes. Longer ones answer 414.
  • The renewal check keeps the CACerts result of at most 1024 path segments, each for 5 minutes.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: This page says what the library protects, what it leaves to the host and what it assumes. Report vulnerabilities privately as SECURITY.md describes.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
• The host runs the router behind its own TLS listener, decides who may enroll with the hooks and owns the CA.
  • The router parses requests, enforces the RFC 7030 renewal rules and the limits and calls the CA.
  • The CA decides what to issue.
  • The client verifies the server, authenticates itself and parses the responses.

docs.title: What the router enforces
docs.text:
• Request format. Bodies must be base64 DER of the expected type and within MaxRequestBody. Request signatures are checked before the CA is called, except for /serverkeygen, which RFC 7030 section 4.4.1 exempts.
  • Renewal identity. A renewal over TLS must present a certificate that chains to the CACerts roots, is valid now and allows client authentication. The request must repeat its Subject and SubjectAltName byte for byte. The system roots are never used for this check.
  • Authentication results. When a hook is set, a request it refuses never reaches the CA.
  • Bounded resources. Request bodies, additional path segments and the CA certificate cache are bounded. RateLimit and Timeout add server-wide limits.
  • No leaked internals. An error that is not an est.Error answers 500 without its text. Panics are recovered.

docs.title: What the host must do
docs.text:
• Configure TLS. The router sees only what http.Request.TLS holds. The listener chooses the protocol versions, the client certificate policy and ClientCAs.
  • Authenticate enrollments. Without hooks every client that completes the handshake may enroll and use /serverkeygen. CheckBearerToken alone does not require a token, see Authentication.
  • Apply issuance policy in the CA. The router does not check which names a request may contain, which key types are allowed or whether a tls-unique challenge password matches the connection.
  • Check revocation. The renewal check does not consult CRLs or OCSP. A CA that revokes must refuse a revoked certificate in Reenroll.
  • Bind password renewals to the signed-in identity. With TLS-SRP or PasswordRenewal, Reenroll receives a nil certificate. The CA must choose the certificate to renew from the username or token, never from the Subject of the request.
  • Protect stored secrets. TLS-SRP needs only verifiers on the server, but passwords for Basic authentication and tokens are checked by the host's own code.
  • Set TrustProxyHeaders only behind a proxy that overwrites the headers. Otherwise clients choose the address in the log.

docs.title: What the client enforces
docs.text:
• The server certificate is verified against ExplicitAnchor, ImplicitAnchor or the system roots, unless InsecureSkipVerify is set. TLS-SRP authenticates the server by the password instead.
  • Redirects are never followed, so credentials do not go to another location.
  • Response bodies are bounded by MaxResponseBody.
  • An enrollment response must carry exactly one certificate unless AllowCertificateChain is set.
  • Control characters in server error messages are escaped, so printing them cannot drive a terminal.
  • TLS-SRP refuses groups below 2048 bits by default.

estclient adds protections for files. Private keys are written with mode 0600, an existing key file loses group and other access before it is written and symbolic links are refused as output paths.

docs.title: Assumptions and limits
docs.text:
• estserver is not a production server. Its mock CA issues to anyone and its operations need no authentication.
  • Proof of possession through tls-unique needs TLS 1.2. TLS 1.3 has no such value, so the binding is absent from every TLS 1.3 connection, including all ML-DSA renewals.
  • InsecureSkipVerify trusts the network. Use it only to fetch CA certificates that you then check out of band.
  • MaxRequestBody must stay below 4 MiB. /tpmenroll decodes its PKCS #7 part with a recursive parser and a body nested deep enough ends the process.
  • Logs. The request log holds the method, the URI, the client address and the status. The router does not log request bodies or credentials. The causes of 500 answers are logged as the CA wrote them.

docs.title: Supported versions
docs.text: Only the latest release receives fixes. See SECURITY.md for the severity tiers and fix targets. Verifying a release shows how to check the release artifacts.

docs.title: Verifying a release
docs.text:
Each GitHub release carries:

  • the complete source tree as go-pki-est-<version>-source.zip and .tar.gz
  • a CycloneDX SBOM, go-pki-est-<version>-sbom.cdx.json
  • the SHA-256 checksums of those three files, go-pki-est-<version>_SHA256SUMS.txt
  • a signed build provenance bundle, go-pki-est-<version>.intoto.jsonl

Check a downloaded file against the checksums, then confirm that the release workflow of this repository built it. --ignore-missing skips the listed files you did not download:

shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing go-pki-est-v1.4.0_SHA256SUMS.txt

gh attestation verify go-pki-est-v1.4.0-source.tar.gz --repo misiektoja/go-pki-est

To verify without network access to the attestation API, add --bundle go-pki-est-v1.4.0.intoto.jsonl.

go get and go install fetch the module through the Go module proxy and check it against the checksum database, so they need none of these files. The archives serve users who build from a downloaded source tree.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The router decides who may run an operation with two optional hooks and checks renewals itself. /cacerts and /csrattrs are always open. The hooks run for /simpleenroll, /simplereenroll, /serverkeygen, /tpmenroll and /healthcheck.

docs.title: The hooks
docs.text:
CheckBearerToken runs for every request that carries Authorization: Bearer <token>. The prefix Bearer is case-sensitive, so a request with bearer <token> counts as one without a token. CheckBasicAuth runs for every other request, with empty credentials when the request has no Basic credentials. That lets it accept a client certificate instead of a password, as the router example in Embedding the server does with r.TLS.VerifiedChains.

Hook result Response nil The request continues An est.Error with a status other than 401, such as 403 or 429 That status, its message and its Retry-After value Any other error 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge and no body

Without hooks, the enrollment operations are open to every client that completes the TLS handshake. The table shows what each combination requires:

Hooks set Request without credentials Request with a bearer token Request with Basic credentials None Accepted Accepted, token ignored Accepted, credentials ignored CheckBasicAuth CheckBasicAuth with empty credentials CheckBasicAuth with empty credentials CheckBasicAuth CheckBearerToken Accepted CheckBearerToken Accepted, credentials ignored Both CheckBasicAuth with empty credentials CheckBearerToken CheckBasicAuth

CheckBearerToken alone does not require a token. Set CheckBasicAuth too and return an error from it to refuse requests that carry no token.

TLS-SRP clients reach the same hooks. SRPUsernameFromContext(ctx) returns their username, see TLS-SRP.

docs.title: The 401 challenge
docs.text:
A refused request gets 401 with no body, because some clients, such as Bouncy Castle, fail when they do not read the content of a challenge. The WWW-Authenticate header names the realm estserver@<host> with the host of the request:

  • Basic realm="estserver@est.example.com" when CheckBasicAuth is set or CheckBearerToken is not
  • Bearer realm="estserver@est.example.com" when CheckBearerToken is set, followed by , error="invalid_token" when the request carried a token

Each challenge is a separate header line. The header name is written as WWW-Authenticate, the RFC 9110 spelling, because libest compares header names case-sensitively.

docs.title: The health check
docs.text: GET /healthcheck answers 200 with an empty body when a hook accepts the request. Unlike the EST operations it is never open: without hooks it always answers 401. estserver accepts it with the Basic user healthcheck and the configured password.

docs.title: Renewal checks
docs.text:
For /simplereenroll the router checks the client certificate before it calls CA.Reenroll:

  1. A certificate must be present, unless the client signed in with TLS-SRP or password renewal applies. Otherwise: 403 client certificate must be provided for /simplereenroll.
  2. The Subject and the SubjectAltName extension of the request must equal those of the certificate, byte for byte (RFC 7030 section 4.2.2). Otherwise: 403 Subject and SubjectAltName fields in CSR must be identical to certificate being renewed.
  3. The certificate must verify against the certificates CA.CACerts returns for the same path segment, at the current time and for client authentication. Otherwise: 403 invalid client certificate. If CACerts itself fails, the request fails with that error.

The router uses the first certificate the client presented, so it works with listeners that request a certificate without verifying it.

docs.title: Custom certificate verification
docs.text: VerifyClientCertificate replaces step 3. Use it for certificates that crypto/x509 cannot verify, such as certificates an SLH-DSA or composite ML-DSA CA signed. Steps 1 and 2 still run first. A nil error accepts the certificate, an est.Error is sent as is and any other error answers 403 invalid client certificate. The listener must use tls.RequestClientCert, see Post-quantum algorithms.

docs.title: Password renewal
docs.text:
RFC 7030 section 2.3 allows a renewal that a password signs in instead of the certificate being renewed, for certificates that cannot authenticate TLS. PasswordRenewal turns this on:

cfg := &est.ServerConfig{
    CheckBasicAuth: func(ctx context.Context, r *http.Request, aps, username, password string) error {
        want, ok := passwords[username]
        if !ok || subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(password), []byte(want)) != 1 {
            return errors.New("unknown user or wrong password")
        }
        return nil
    },
    PasswordRenewal: true,
}
  • A renewal without a client certificate is accepted when CheckBasicAuth accepted Basic credentials with a non-empty username or CheckBearerToken accepted a token. A bearer token counts only when CheckBearerToken is set.
  • NewRouter refuses PasswordRenewal without either hook.
  • A client that does present a certificate still goes through all three renewal checks.
  • CA.Reenroll receives a nil certificate and must choose the certificate to renew by the signed-in identity, never by the Subject of the request. The CA in The CA interface compares the requested common name with the username.

PasswordRenewal is off by default.

docs.title: Proof of possession
docs.text: The router does not check the tls-unique challenge password that a client adds with SigningKey. A CA that requires the binding compares the challenge password in the request with the tls-unique value of the connection, which r.TLS.TLSUnique holds for TLS 1.2. Over TLS-SRP r.TLS is nil, so the host passes the value of the go-tls-srp connection to the CA itself, for example in the request context.

docs.title: The CA interface
docs.text: The router hands every EST operation that passed its checks to a value that implements est.CA. That value is your CA: it may sign in process, call a CA over the network or queue a request for an operator.

docs.title: A minimal CA
docs.text:
This CA signs every request with an in-memory root. It is the CA of the examples in example_test.go. Its issue helper, which signs with x509.CreateCertificate, is in the same file:

// caError is an error with an HTTP status. The server sends its status, message and Retry-After
// value to the client.
type caError struct {
    status     int
    msg        string
    retryAfter int
}

// Error returns the message sent to the client.
func (e caError) Error() string { return e.msg }

// StatusCode returns the HTTP status of the response.
func (e caError) StatusCode() int { return e.status }

// RetryAfter returns the Retry-After value in seconds, or 0 for none.
func (e caError) RetryAfter() int { return e.retryAfter }

// CACerts returns the certificates clients use as trust anchors.
func (ca *exampleCA) CACerts(ctx context.Context, aps string, r *http.Request) ([]*x509.Certificate, error) {
    return []*x509.Certificate{ca.root}, nil
}

// CSRAttrs asks clients for a P-384 key, using the example of RFC 7030 section 4.5.2.
func (ca *exampleCA) CSRAttrs(ctx context.Context, aps string, r *http.Request) (est.CSRAttrs, error) {
    return est.CSRAttrs{
        Attributes: []est.Attribute{{
            Type:   asn1.ObjectIdentifier{1, 2, 840, 10045, 2, 1},
            Values: est.AttributeValueSET{asn1.ObjectIdentifier{1, 3, 132, 0, 34}},
        }},
    }, nil
}

// Enroll issues a certificate for the key in the request.
func (ca *exampleCA) Enroll(ctx context.Context, csr *x509.CertificateRequest, aps string, r *http.Request) (*x509.Certificate, error) {
    return ca.issue(csr, csr.PublicKey)
}

// Reenroll renews a certificate. cert is nil when the client signed in with TLS-SRP or, with
// PasswordRenewal, with a password or bearer token instead of the certificate being renewed.
func (ca *exampleCA) Reenroll(ctx context.Context, cert *x509.Certificate, csr *x509.CertificateRequest, aps string, r *http.Request) (*x509.Certificate, error) {
    if cert == nil {
        // Any client can name any subject in a CSR, so the renewal is tied to the signed-in user.
        user := est.SRPUsernameFromContext(ctx)
        if user == "" {
            user, _, _ = r.BasicAuth()
        }
        if user == "" || csr.Subject.CommonName != user {
            return nil, caError{status: http.StatusForbidden, msg: "renewal is limited to the signed-in user"}
        }
    }
    return ca.issue(csr, csr.PublicKey)
}

// ServerKeyGen generates a key for the client and returns it unencrypted as PKCS #8.
func (ca *exampleCA) ServerKeyGen(ctx context.Context, csr *x509.CertificateRequest, aps string, r *http.Request) (*x509.Certificate, []byte, error) {
    key, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    // The server ignores the key and the signature of the request, so only its names are used.
    cert, err := ca.issue(csr, key.Public())
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    der, err := x509.MarshalPKCS8PrivateKey(key)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    return cert, der, nil
}

// TPMEnroll refuses TPM enrollment, which this CA does not offer.
func (ca *exampleCA) TPMEnroll(ctx context.Context, csr *x509.CertificateRequest, ekcerts []*x509.Certificate, ekPub, akPub []byte, aps string, r *http.Request) ([]byte, []byte, []byte, error) {
    return nil, nil, nil, caError{status: http.StatusNotImplemented, msg: "TPM enrollment is not offered"}
}

docs.title: What every method receives
docs.text:
• ctx is the request context. LoggerFromContext(ctx) returns the server logger and SRPUsernameFromContext(ctx) the TLS-SRP username, if any. It ends when the client disconnects or ServerConfig.Timeout passes.
  • aps is the additional path segment of the request or empty. Use it to select one of several CAs or profiles.
  • r is the HTTP request. It carries the headers, the Host, the Basic credentials and the TLS state. The router has already read the body of a POST request.

docs.title: CACerts
docs.text:
Returns the CA certificates for /cacerts. The router sends them in the order returned and also uses them to check client certificates on renewal: self-signed certificates become the trusted roots and all others intermediates. Include the root. Without a self-signed certificate no client certificate verifies and every renewal over TLS answers 403 invalid client certificate. The system roots are never used for this check.

For the renewal check the router caches the result per additional path segment for 5 minutes and for at most 1024 segments. A /cacerts request also replaces a cached entry older than that.

docs.title: CSRAttrs
docs.text: Returns the attributes for /csrattrs. An empty value is sent as an empty sequence with status 200.

docs.title: Enroll
docs.text: Issues a certificate for /simpleenroll. The request is parsed and its signature is checked before the call. Everything else is policy for the CA: which names it allows, which key types and whether a tls-unique challenge password must match the TLS session. Return exactly one certificate.

docs.title: Reenroll
docs.text:
Renews a certificate for /simplereenroll. cert is the TLS client certificate being renewed. The router has checked that the request repeats its Subject and SubjectAltName and that the certificate chains to the CACerts roots, is within its validity period and allows client authentication. With VerifyClientCertificate set, that hook decides instead of the chain check.

  • The router does not check revocation. A CA that revokes certificates must refuse a revoked cert here.
  • cert is nil when the client signed in with TLS-SRP or, with PasswordRenewal, with a password or bearer token. The CA must then choose the certificate to renew by the signed-in identity, never by the Subject of the request, which any client can name. The example above shows one way.
  • A ChangeSubjectName attribute (RFC 7030 section 4.2.2) stays in the request the CA receives. The router does not act on it and the Subject and SubjectAltName of the request must still match the certificate.

docs.title: ServerKeyGen
docs.text:
Generates a key and issues a certificate for /serverkeygen. The router does not check the request signature, as RFC 7030 section 4.4.1 requires, so use only the names of the request. Return the key in one of two forms:

  • PKCS #8 DER to send it unencrypted. The router recognizes PKCS #8 by its structure, so keys that crypto/x509 cannot parse, such as ML-KEM, are sent as they are.
  • A CMS SignedData inside an EnvelopedData to send it encrypted. The router sends anything that parses as PKCS #7 with smime-type=server-generated-key.

Any other bytes answer 500.

docs.title: TPMEnroll
docs.text: Issues a certificate for /tpmenroll and returns the encrypted credential, the encrypted seed and the certificate inside a CMS EnvelopedData encrypted with the credential. See TPM enrollment. A CA that does not offer it returns an error such as 501, as the example does.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
An error that implements est.Error sets the response:

Method Effect StatusCode() The HTTP status, such as 400, 403, 202 or 503 Error() The reason, sent as the text body <status> <reason> followed by a newline RetryAfter() The Retry-After header in seconds, sent when it is above 0

Any other error answers 500 internal server error and is logged with its text, so the client never sees internal details. A 500 from an est.Error is logged too. A panic in the CA is recovered, logged with its stack and answered with 500.

To defer an enrollment, for example until an operator approves it, return status 202 with a Retry-After value. The client returns both to its caller, see Deferred and refused requests. The router keeps no state, so the CA must recognize the repeated request itself, for example by its public key.

docs.title: Embedding the server
docs.text: NewRouter builds an http.Handler that serves EST in front of your CA. You supply the CA as an implementation of the CA interface, decide who may enroll with the authentication hooks and serve the handler with your own http.Server.

docs.title: A complete server
docs.text:
// One-time enrollment passwords, as an operator would issue them.
passwords := map[string]string{"device-1": "one-time-secret"}

router, err := est.NewRouter(&est.ServerConfig{
    CA:        ca,
    RateLimit: 50,
    CheckBasicAuth: func(ctx context.Context, r *http.Request, aps, username, password string) error {
        // A client certificate that crypto/tls verified needs no password.
        if r.TLS != nil && len(r.TLS.VerifiedChains) > 0 {
            return nil
        }
        want, ok := passwords[username]
        if !ok || subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(password), []byte(want)) != 1 {
            return errors.New("unknown user or wrong password")
        }
        return nil
    },
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

clientCAs := x509.NewCertPool()
clientCAs.AddCert(ca.root)

srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:    ":8443",
    Handler: router,
    TLSConfig: &tls.Config{
        MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12,
        ClientAuth: tls.VerifyClientCertIfGiven,
        ClientCAs:  clientCAs,
    },
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 30 * time.Second,
}
log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("server-chain.pem", "server-key.pem"))

This is ExampleNewRouter in example_test.go, which go test compiles. The example CA in The CA interface stands in for yours.

  • NewRouter fails when PasswordRenewal is set without CheckBasicAuth or CheckBearerToken or when MaxRequestBody or RateLimit is negative. Every other field has a working default.
  • The router reads the client certificate from http.Request.TLS, so it must run on the server that terminates TLS. A reverse proxy in front that terminates TLS hides the certificate and renewals fail with 403.

docs.title: The TLS listener
docs.text:
The router does not configure TLS. Set up the listener for the clients you expect:

  • ClientAuth: tls.VerifyClientCertIfGiven asks for a certificate without requiring one, so one port serves a first enrollment with a password and a renewal with a certificate. RequireAndVerifyClientCert suits deployments where every client already has a certificate.
  • ClientCAs holds the roots that client certificates must chain to. Go clients, including est.Client, pick the certificate to present by these names, so a client whose certificate comes from an intermediate must send that intermediate, see Renewing a certificate.
  • TLS 1.2 must stay enabled for clients that bind requests with tls-unique, which TLS 1.3 does not have.
  • tls.RequestClientCert is needed with VerifyClientCertificate, because crypto/tls would otherwise refuse a certificate it cannot verify before the router sees it. See Post-quantum algorithms.

TLS-SRP needs a listener from go-tls-srp instead of crypto/tls.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method and path Request body Response Authentication GET /.well-known/est/cacerts None application/pkcs7-mime None GET /.well-known/est/csrattrs None application/csrattrs None POST /.well-known/est/simpleenroll application/pkcs10 application/pkcs7-mime; smime-type=certs-only Hooks, optional without them POST /.well-known/est/simplereenroll application/pkcs10 application/pkcs7-mime; smime-type=certs-only Hooks, plus the renewal checks POST /.well-known/est/serverkeygen application/pkcs10 multipart/mixed with the key and the certificate Hooks, optional without them POST /.well-known/est/tpmenroll multipart/mixed multipart/mixed with three parts Hooks, optional without them GET /healthcheck None 200 with an empty body Hooks, always required
  • Every EST path also exists with an additional path segment, such as /.well-known/est/devices/simpleenroll. The CA receives the segment as aps. A segment longer than 255 bytes answers 414.
  • Bodies are base64 in both directions. The router writes 76-character lines and accepts spaces, tabs, CR and LF in a request.
  • "Optional without them" means the operation is open when neither CheckBasicAuth nor CheckBearerToken is set. /healthcheck then always answers 401.
  • An unknown path answers 404. A known path with the wrong method answers 405 with an Allow header.

Mount the router so that it receives the full path, for example with mux.Handle("/.well-known/est/", router) and mux.Handle("/healthcheck", router). Do not strip a prefix.

docs.title: Response headers
docs.text:
Every response carries:

  • Server: go-pki-est EST server v1.4.0, with the library version
  • Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000, unless OmitStrictTransportSecurity is set
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

Base64 response bodies and the parts of multipart responses also carry Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, which RFC 8951 tells receivers to ignore. Set OmitTransferEncoding for clients that fail when it is present. Error responses are text/plain; charset=utf-8.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Logger receives one entry per request, after the response, with the method, URI, protocol, remote address, status, bytes written, time taken and request ID. Responses with status 500 are logged at error level with their cause and so are recovered panics with their stack. The CA reads the same logger with LoggerFromContext(ctx). Without a logger nothing is logged.

The Logger interface has Errorf, Errorw, Infof, Infow and With. The request ID comes from chi's RequestID middleware, which reuses an incoming X-Request-Id header.

docs.title: Behind a load balancer
docs.text:
• TrustProxyHeaders sets r.RemoteAddr from X-Real-IP or else from the first address in X-Forwarded-For, so the logs, the hooks, the refusal recorder and the CA all see that address. True-Client-IP is ignored. Enable it only when every request passes a proxy that removes or overwrites both headers. The proxy's own address is not checked.
  • AllowedHosts refuses requests whose Host header names another host with 400 host not allowed. Names compare without case and without the port. IPv6 addresses may be listed with or without brackets.

A load balancer that passes TCP through keeps client certificates working. One that terminates TLS does not, as noted above.

docs.title: Refusals and limits
docs.text: The router refuses some requests itself, before or instead of calling the CA. This page lists those refusals, how to record them and the limits that protect the server.

docs.title: Requests the router refuses
docs.text:
Status Message Cause 400 host not allowed The Host header names a host that AllowedHosts does not list 400 invalid base64 encoding The body is not base64 400 malformed PKCS10 certificate signing request The body is not a PKCS #10 request 400 invalid PKCS10 certificate signing request signature The request signature does not verify 400 unsupported PKCS10 certificate signing request signature algorithm crypto/x509 cannot verify the signature algorithm or CheckCSRSignature returned x509.ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm 403 client certificate must be provided for /simplereenroll A renewal without a certificate, TLS-SRP or password renewal 403 Subject and SubjectAltName fields in CSR must be identical to certificate being renewed A renewal that changes the names 403 invalid client certificate The renewal certificate does not verify 413 request body too large The body is larger than MaxRequestBody 414 additional path segment too long The additional path segment is longer than 255 bytes 415 Content-Type must be application/pkcs10 A POST with another content type. /tpmenroll asks for multipart/mixed 415 malformed or missing Content-Type header A POST without a valid Content-Type 429 rate limit exceeded More requests than RateLimit allows, with Retry-After: 1

/tpmenroll adds its own checks of the multipart body and the TPM public areas, such as 422 public key in public area doesn't match. See TPM enrollment.

The body of a refusal is the text <status> <message> and a newline. A request for an unknown path answers 404 and a known path with the wrong method 405. Authentication failures answer as Authentication describes.

docs.title: Recording refusals
docs.text:
ServerConfig.Refusals receives every refusal in the table above, so a host can count them, log them in its own format or alert on them:

// printRefusals prints each request the server refuses without asking the CA.
type printRefusals struct{}

// RecordRefusal prints the operation, the status and the reason.
func (printRefusals) RecordRefusal(ctx context.Context, refusal est.Refusal) error {
    fmt.Printf("refused %s: %d %s\n", refusal.Operation, refusal.Status, refusal.Reason)
    return nil
}

ExampleRefusalRecorder in example_test.go sends a renewal without a client certificate and prints:

refused simplereenroll: 403 client certificate must be provided for /simplereenroll
client: 403 client certificate must be provided for /simplereenroll
  • Refusal holds the operation, such as simpleenroll, the additional path segment, the status, the message and the request. The body of the request may already have been read.
  • RecordRefusal runs before the response is written, with a context that the client cannot cancel. Bound its work, because the client waits for it.
  • An error from RecordRefusal is logged and does not change the response.
  • The recorder does not receive refusals from CheckBasicAuth and CheckBearerToken or errors from the CA. It does receive refusals from CheckCSRSignature and VerifyClientCertificate. It never receives answers with status 500 or higher.

docs.title: Request size
docs.text: MaxRequestBody bounds the body of a POST request, 64 KiB by default. A larger body answers 413. Raise it for large post-quantum requests: an SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f request takes about 67 KB in base64. Keep it below 4 MiB, because /tpmenroll decodes its PKCS #7 part with a parser that recurses once per nested structure and a body nested deep enough ends the process. NewRouter refuses a negative value.

docs.title: Request rate
docs.text:
RateLimit limits all requests to the router together, in requests per second, with bursts of up to twice that number. It is one limit for all clients, not one per client. A request over the limit answers 429 with Retry-After: 1. Without RateLimit there is no limit. NewRouter refuses a negative value.

For limits per client or per account, return an est.Error with status 429 and a Retry-After value from a hook. A TLS-SRP server can refuse a client before the costly handshake, see TLS-SRP.

docs.title: Request time
docs.text:
Timeout cancels the request context after the given time, 60 seconds by default. The router does not stop a CA that ignores the context. A CA that returns the context error answers 500, because that error is not an est.Error. Return an est.Error with status 503 or 504 to give the client another status.

Set the timeouts of the http.Server too. ReadHeaderTimeout limits slow clients before the router sees the request.

docs.title: Additional path segments
docs.text: A segment may be at most 255 bytes. The router keeps the CACerts result of at most 1024 segments for its renewal check. Any client can add an entry through /cacerts, so the bound keeps random segments from filling memory.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text: AllowedHosts refuses requests whose Host header names another host with 400 host not allowed. Names compare without case and without the port. IPv6 addresses may be listed with or without brackets. Without AllowedHosts every host name is accepted.

docs.title: TLS-SRP
docs.text:
RFC 7030 section 3.3.3 lets a client sign in with TLS-SRP (RFC 5054) instead of a certificate. The client proves that it knows a password and the server proves that it holds the verifier made from that password, so neither side needs a certificate. This suits devices that are provisioned with a username and password and have no trust anchor yet.

The TLS-SRP stack is go-tls-srp, a trimmed copy of crypto/tls with the SRP cipher suites only. It runs TLS 1.2 without certificates, session resumption or renegotiation.

docs.title: Serving EST over TLS-SRP
docs.text:
The router stays the same. Only the listener and a small handler around the router change:

// A real host stores the salt and verifier when it registers the device, never the password.
group, err := srptls.GroupByBits(3072)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
salt, err := srptls.NewSalt(rand.Reader)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
verifier, err := srptls.NewVerifier(group, []byte("device-5"), []byte("srp-secret"), salt)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

ln, err := srptls.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0", &srptls.Config{
    GetVerifier: func(info *srptls.ClientHelloInfo) (*srptls.Verifier, error) {
        if info.Username != "device-5" {
            return nil, srptls.ErrUnknownUsername
        }
        return verifier, nil
    },
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

router, err := est.NewRouter(&est.ServerConfig{
    CA: ca,
    CheckBasicAuth: func(ctx context.Context, r *http.Request, aps, username, password string) error {
        if est.SRPUsernameFromContext(ctx) == "" {
            return errors.New("sign in with TLS-SRP")
        }
        return nil
    },
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

srv := &http.Server{
    // net/http sets Request.TLS only for crypto/tls, so the handler reads the TLS-SRP
    // connection from the context and passes the username to the router.
    Handler: http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        conn, ok := r.Context().Value(srpConnKey{}).(*srptls.Conn)
        if !ok {
            http.Error(w, "no TLS-SRP connection", http.StatusInternalServerError)
            return
        }
        ctx := est.WithSRPUsername(r.Context(), conn.ConnectionState().SRPUsername)
        router.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))
    }),
    ConnContext: func(ctx context.Context, c net.Conn) context.Context {
        return context.WithValue(ctx, srpConnKey{}, c)
    },
    // net/http logs handshake failures only for crypto/tls. Handshake returns the stored
    // error of a failed handshake.
    ConnState: func(c net.Conn, state http.ConnState) {
        conn, ok := c.(*srptls.Conn)
        if !ok || state != http.StateClosed || conn.ConnectionState().HandshakeComplete {
            return
        }
        if err := conn.Handshake(); err != nil {
            log.Printf("TLS-SRP handshake from %s failed: %v", c.RemoteAddr(), err)
        }
    },
    // The handshake runs in the first read, so this also bounds it.
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 30 * time.Second,
}
go func() { _ = srv.Serve(ln) }()

This is ExampleWithSRPUsername in example_test.go. The client side of the same example is in Signing in.

  • GetVerifier returns the stored verifier of the username in the ClientHello. It is the only required field of srptls.Config on the server.
  • ConnContext and the handler pass the username to the router. net/http sets Request.TLS only for crypto/tls connections, so r.TLS stays nil and the handler reads the username from the go-tls-srp connection. est.WithSRPUsername stores it in the request context.
  • The hooks run as for any other client. est.SRPUsernameFromContext(ctx) returns the username and CheckBasicAuth receives empty credentials unless the client also sent HTTP Basic credentials. Without hooks every client that completes the handshake may enroll.
  • Renewal needs no client certificate. The router skips its certificate checks and CA.Reenroll receives a nil certificate. The CA must choose the certificate to renew by the username, never by the Subject of the request. See The CA interface.
  • Log entries show the scheme https for TLS-SRP requests, the same as for TLS.

A server can offer TLS and TLS-SRP on two ports with the same router, as estserver does.

docs.title: Storing verifiers
docs.text:
Store the group, the salt and the verifier of each user when you register the device. The server never needs the password:

  • srptls.GroupByBits returns one of the seven RFC 5054 groups: 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072, 4096, 6144 or 8192 bits. Clients that use go-tls-srp, including est.Client, refuse groups below 2048 bits unless SRPMinGroupBits allows them.
  • srptls.NewSalt returns a 20-byte random salt without a leading zero byte, which OpenSSL clients would drop.
  • srptls.NewVerifier computes the verifier as RFC 5054 section 2.4 describes, with the username and password hashed as given.

Verifier.Validate checks a stored record against the limits of RFC 5054 and its group. Use it when you load verifiers from storage.

docs.title: Verifiers from OpenSSL
docs.text:
openssl srp creates verifier files that OpenSSL and estserver read. The file must exist before the first user is added:

touch srpvfile
openssl srp -srpvfile srpvfile -add -gn 3072 device-1

The command asks for the password. -delete marks a user as revoked with an R line. estserver skips revoked users and reads I lines that define a group by its parameters, as long as the group is one of the RFC 5054 groups. See estserver for the file format.

docs.title: Unknown usernames
docs.text:
GetVerifier decides what a client with an unknown username learns:

GetVerifier returns The handshake fails with The client learns srptls.ErrUnknownUsername An unknown_psk_identity alert That the username does not exist srptls.SimulatedVerifier(seed, group, username) A bad_record_mac alert, as for a wrong password Nothing about which usernames exist srptls.ErrAccessDenied An access_denied alert, before the costly SRP computation That it was refused
  • SimulatedVerifier gives the same salt for the same seed and username, so repeated attempts look like a real user. Use a long random seed that stays the same across restarts and on every server that answers the same clients. Pick the group most of your users have, so the group does not give unknown users away.
  • ErrAccessDenied suits a rate limit. The SRP computation runs in the handshake, before the router and its RateLimit see the request.
  • Any other error from GetVerifier aborts the handshake with an internal_error alert.

The client reports these cases with the errors listed in Signing in.

docs.title: Cipher suites
docs.text: The server picks the first suite in srptls.Config.CipherSuites that the client offers. The default is TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA, then TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA is used only when it is listed. The suites that also sign with a server certificate are not implemented.

docs.title: Handshake failures
docs.text:
net/http logs handshake failures only for crypto/tls. Without help a failed TLS-SRP handshake closes the connection without a log entry. The ConnState function in the example above checks each connection when it closes and logs the error of a handshake that did not complete. estserver does the same at info level, for example TLS-SRP handshake from 127.0.0.1:53110 failed: remote error: tls: insufficient security level when the client refused a group that was too small.

Set ReadHeaderTimeout on the http.Server. The handshake runs in the first read of the connection, so this timeout also bounds it.

docs.title: estclient
docs.text:
estclient is a command line EST client built on the library. It fetches CA certificates and CSR attributes, enrolls, renews and asks the server to generate a key. It signs with keys in files, on a PKCS #11 HSM or on a TPM 2.0 device.

go install github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est/cmd/estclient@latest

Getting started walks through a full session against estserver.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
estclient <command> [options]
Command Operation cacerts Fetch the CA certificates (RFC 7030 section 4.1) csrattrs Fetch the CSR attributes the CA wants (section 4.5) csr Generate a PKCS #10 request locally, without a server enroll Request a new certificate (section 4.2) reenroll Renew a certificate (section 4.2) serverkeygen Request a key and a certificate from the server (section 4.4) tpmenroll Request a certificate for a TPM key, see tpmenroll sampleconfig Print a sample configuration file version Print the version, such as go-pki-est EST client 1.4.0 help Print the command list. estclient help -common describes the common options

estclient <command> -help lists the options of a command. On failure the tool prints estclient: <error> to standard error and exits with status 1. An unknown option prints the usage of the command and exits with status 2.

docs.title: Connection options
docs.text:
The commands that talk to a server share these options:

Option Meaning -server <host:port> The EST server. Required, here or in the configuration file -aps <string> The additional path segment, such as devices in /.well-known/est/devices/simpleenroll -explicit <path> PEM file with the CA certificates that verify the server (RFC 7030 section 3.6.1) -implicit <path> PEM file used when no explicit anchor is set. Without either, the system roots apply -insecure Accept any server certificate. Command line only, see Bootstrapping -certs <path> PEM file with the TLS client certificate first, then the CA certificates the server needs to build the chain -key <path> PEM file with the private key of the client certificate or the key that signs a generated request -user <string>, -pass <string> HTTP Basic credentials -token <string> HTTP bearer token. -user takes precedence -headers <string> Extra HTTP headers as Name:value items, separated by -separator -hostheader <string> Override the HTTP Host header -proxy <url> HTTP or HTTPS proxy. Without it HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY apply -timeout <duration> Time limit for the request, 15s by default -separator <string> Separator of list values, , by default -config <path> Configuration file -out <path> Output file. Standard output by default. csrattrs always prints to standard output

When both anchors are given, only the explicit one is used.

docs.title: cacerts
docs.text:
estclient cacerts -server est.example.com:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -out cacerts.pem

Writes the CA certificates in PEM, in the order the server sent them. Filters:

  • -roots keeps the self-signed certificates.
  • -intermediates keeps all others.
  • -rootout keeps the first self-signed certificate and fails with failed to find a root certificate in CA certificates when there is none. The help text marks it for deprecation in favor of -roots.
  • -separate writes each certificate to its own file. With -out chain.pem the files are chain-1.pem, chain-2.pem and so on. Without -out they are ca-1.pem, ca-2.pem.

Only one of -roots, -intermediates and -rootout may be given.

docs.title: csrattrs
docs.text:
estclient csrattrs -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -aps csrattrs

Prints each attribute the server asks for. Against estserver with the csrattrs path segment:

OID     : 1.2.840.113549.1.9.7
OID     : 1.2.840.10045.4.3.3
Type    : 1.2.840.113549.1.9.14
 Value  : 1.3.6.1.1.1.1.22
Type    : 1.2.840.10045.2.1
 Value  : 1.3.132.0.34

An OID line is an attribute or algorithm the CA wants. A Type line is an attribute with the values that follow it. An empty answer prints nothing.

docs.title: csr
docs.text:
estclient csr -key key.pem -cn 'John Doe' -emails 'john@doe.com' -out csr.pem

Generates a request signed with -key or with the configured key. These options set its fields:

Option Field -cn Subject common name -sn Subject serial number -org, -ou Subject organization and organizational unit -country, -province, -locality, -street, -postalcode Subject address -dnsnames, -emails, -ips, -uris Subject alternative names

-ou, -dnsnames, -emails, -ips and -uris take several values separated by -separator.

docs.title: enroll
docs.text:
estclient enroll -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -csr csr.pem -out cert.pem

Sends the request in -csr. Without -csr it builds one from the csr options and signs it with the key. Without a key it fails with no private key provided.

-signingkey <path> sets a separate key for the request. The client then adds the tls-unique value of the TLS 1.2 connection as the challenge password and signs the request with that key, as RFC 7030 section 3.5 describes. Over TLS 1.3 nothing is added.

docs.title: reenroll
docs.text:
estclient reenroll -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -key key.pem -certs certs.pem -out newcert.pem

Presents the certificate in -certs and its key in the TLS handshake. Without -certs it fails with no client certificate provided. Without -csr it copies the subject and the subject alternative names of the first certificate in -certs into a new request and signs it with -key. A renewal with a new key therefore needs -csr.

docs.title: serverkeygen
docs.text:
estclient serverkeygen -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -cn 'Jane Doe' -out jane.pem -keyout jane-key.pem

Writes the certificate to -out and the key to -keyout, both to standard output by default. The key is written as a PRIVATE KEY block when it is PKCS #8 or as a PKCS7 block when the server encrypted it. Any other key fails with unrecognized private key format.

Without -csr the request is signed with a new temporary P-256 key, because the server ignores the key in the request.

docs.title: tpmenroll
docs.text:
estclient tpmenroll -config tpm.cfg -server est.example.com:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -out cert.pem

Requests a certificate for a key on a TPM 2.0 device, as TPM enrollment describes. The tool reads the public areas of the key and the endorsement key from the TPM, sends the request, activates the returned credential on the TPM and writes the decrypted certificate.

The key must be a TPM key in the configuration file. It also needs the endorsement key handle (ek_handle) and its certificates (ek_certs or -ekcerts <path>). Missing parts fail with errors such as no endorsement key certificate(s) provided or private key in configuration file is not a TPM private key.

No test runs this command against a TPM. The library tests run /tpmenroll against the mock CA and decrypt the credential in software.

docs.title: sampleconfig
docs.text: Prints a sample configuration file. -hsm prints one with an HSM key and -tpm one with a TPM key. -out writes it to a file.

docs.title: Configuration file
docs.text:
Most options can be set in a JSON file given with -config. Options on the command line override the file. -headers replaces the whole additional_headers map.

{
    "server": "est.fake.domain:8443",
    "additional_path_segment": "someseg",
    "additional_headers": {
        "Certificate-Template": "my-template",
        "Bit-Size": "3072"
    },
    "host_header": "est.fake.host",
    "username": "someuser",
    "password": "somepass",
    "private_key": "test_key.pem"
}
Field Option server -server additional_path_segment -aps additional_headers -headers host_header -hostheader username, password -user, -pass token -token proxy -proxy explicit_anchor, implicit_anchor -explicit, -implicit client_certificates -certs private_key -key or an hsm or tpm object signing_key -signingkey or an hsm or tpm object
  • A relative -config path is looked up in the current directory, then in the directory that ESTCLIENT_CONFIG_DIRECTORY names when it is an absolute path, then in the home directory.
  • Relative paths inside the file are relative to the directory of the file. Relative paths on the command line are relative to the current directory.
  • -insecure, -timeout, -csr, the subject options such as -cn and the output options -out, -keyout, -separate, -separator, -roots, -rootout and -intermediates have no key in the file.
  • When signing_key is set, enroll, csr and tpmenroll sign the requests they generate with it instead of private_key. reenroll signs with private_key and serverkeygen with a temporary P-256 key.

docs.title: Key files
docs.text: -key and private_key read a PEM file with a PRIVATE KEY (PKCS #8), RSA PRIVATE KEY or EC PRIVATE KEY block. PKCS #8 covers RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519 and ML-DSA keys. A block encrypted in the legacy PEM format, with a Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED header, prompts for the passphrase. An ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY block is refused.

docs.title: Hardware keys
docs.text:
HSM and TPM keys can only be set in the configuration file. They work as the TLS client key and as the key that signs generated requests.

An HSM key is reached through PKCS #11:

"private_key": {
    "hsm": {
        "pkcs11_library_path": "/usr/local/lib/softhsm/libsofthsm2.so",
        "token_label": "Testing Token",
        "token_pin": "1234",
        "key_id": 1
    }
}

When token_pin is empty, the tool asks for the PIN on the terminal. CI runs the HSM tests with SoftHSM on Linux.

docs.title: TPM keys
docs.text:
"private_key": {
    "tpm": {
        "device": "/dev/tpmrm0",
        "persistent_handle": 2164391936,
        "storage_handle": 2164260865,
        "ek_handle": 2164326401,
        "key_password": "xyzzy",
        "storage_password": "opensesame",
        "ek_password": "abracadabra",
        "ek_certs": "/path/to/ek/certs/chain.pem",
        "public_area": "signing_key.pub",
        "private_area": "signing_key.priv"
    }
}

The key is loaded from persistent_handle when it is set. Otherwise it is loaded under storage_handle from the public_area and private_area files. ek_handle and ek_certs are needed by tpmenroll only.

docs.title: Bootstrapping
docs.text:
-insecure skips the check of the server certificate. Use it once to fetch the CA certificates of a new server, check them out of band, for example by their fingerprint and use them as -explicit from then on:

estclient cacerts -server localhost:8443 -insecure -roots -out anchor.pem

openssl x509 -in anchor.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256

This does not work when the server certificate does not come from the EST CA, because the fetched roots then cannot verify the server.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
• Certificates are written in PEM. New files get mode 0666 and private keys 0600, both reduced by the umask.
  • An existing file is truncated. On Unix it first loses any permission that a new file would not get, so an existing key file ends up readable by its owner only.
  • An output path that is a symbolic link is refused with output file link.pem is a symbolic link, name its target instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• estclient has no TLS-SRP options. Use the library's SRPUsername and SRPPassword instead.
  • It does not show the Retry-After value of a deferred request. The error reads, for example, failed to get certificate: 202 triggered deferred response.
  • It has no option for AllowCertificateChain or MaxResponseBody, so the library defaults apply.

docs.title: estserver
docs.text:
estserver serves EST in front of a mock CA. It is for testing clients and for development, not for production: the mock CA issues a certificate to every client that asks.

go install github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-est/cmd/estserver@latest

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
estserver [-config <path>] [-sampleconfig] [-version] [-help]

Without -config the server needs no files:

  • It creates a new mock CA in memory, a root named Non-Production Testing Root CA <random> and an intermediate that issues. Both live for 24 hours and are gone when the server stops.
  • It issues itself a TLS certificate for Testing Non-Production EST Server with the names localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1.
  • It listens on localhost:8443, logs to standard error and accepts client certificates issued under its root.

It logs Starting EST server FOR NON-PRODUCTION USE ONLY when it starts and stops on SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGQUIT or SIGHUP. -version prints go-pki-est EST server 1.4.0 for that release.

docs.title: Configuration file
docs.text:
-sampleconfig prints every field:

{
    "mock_ca": {
        "certificates": "/path/to/CA/certificates.pem",
        "private_key": "/path/to/CA/private/key.pem"
    },
    "tls": {
        "listen_address": "localhost:8443",
        "certificates": "/path/to/server/certificates.pem",
        "private_key": "/path/to/server/private/key.pem",
        "client_cas": [
            "/path/to/first/client/CA/root/certificate.pem",
            "/path/to/second/client/CA/root/certificate.pem",
            "/path/to/third/client/CA/root/certificate.pem"
        ]
    },
    "tls_srp": {
        "listen_address": "localhost:8444",
        "verifier_file": "/path/to/srpvfile",
        "unknown_user_seed": "a long random string kept across restarts"
    },
    "allowed_hosts": [
        "localhost",
        "127.0.0.1",
        "[::1]"
    ],
    "healthcheck_password": "xyzzy",
    "rate_limit": 150,
    "timeout": 30,
    "trust_proxy_headers": false,
    "log_file": "/path/to/log.file"
}

Every field is optional, but a mock_ca or tls section needs both of its files. Relative paths are relative to the current directory. Unknown keys are ignored, so a misspelled key has no effect. The file has no options for MaxRequestBody, PasswordRenewal, CheckBearerToken, OmitTransferEncoding or OmitStrictTransportSecurity, which keep their defaults.

Field Meaning mock_ca.certificates PEM file with the CA certificates. The first one issues and the file should end with the root, because clients and the renewal check need it mock_ca.private_key PEM file with the key of the first certificate tls.listen_address Address of the TLS listener, localhost:8443 by default. It is part of the tls section, so serving other hosts also takes your own certificate, key and client_cas tls.certificates, tls.private_key PEM files with the server certificate chain and its key. Required in a tls section tls.client_cas PEM files with the roots that client certificates must chain to tls_srp A second listener with TLS-SRP, see TLS-SRP allowed_hosts ServerConfig.AllowedHosts. Other Host headers answer 400 host not allowed healthcheck_password Password of the Basic user healthcheck for /healthcheck. Empty by default rate_limit ServerConfig.RateLimit in requests per second for all clients together. 0 means no limit timeout ServerConfig.Timeout in seconds. 0 means 60 seconds trust_proxy_headers ServerConfig.TrustProxyHeaders, false by default log_file Append the request log to this file, created with mode 0644. Standard error by default. Startup errors and TLS handshake errors always go to standard error
  • A tls section without client_cas accepts no client certificate. A renewal then fails in the handshake. The client reports remote error: tls: unknown certificate authority and the server prints an http: TLS handshake error with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority on standard error, also when log_file is set. Without a tls section the server trusts the root of its mock CA.
  • The TLS listener requires TLS 1.2 or newer, asks for a client certificate without requiring one and offers the curves P-521, P-384 and P-256 only. It does not offer the hybrid ML-KEM key exchanges.
  • The HTTP server allows 30 seconds for the request headers, 60 seconds for the whole request and closes idle connections after 120 seconds.
  • Every EST operation is open. The server asks for no password and issues to any client that completes the handshake. Only /healthcheck needs the Basic user healthcheck. Without a configured password, curl -u healthcheck: passes it.
  • trust_proxy_headers takes the client address for the log from X-Real-IP or else from X-Forwarded-For. Enable it only when every request passes a proxy that removes or overwrites both headers. The server does not check the address of the proxy.

docs.title: The mock CA
docs.text:
Every certificate the mock CA issues:

  • is valid for 90 days or until its CA expires if that comes first
  • has a random 128-bit serial number
  • copies the subject and the subject alternative names from the request byte for byte
  • allows digital signatures, server authentication and client authentication and is not a CA

A renewal is issued the same way. The mock CA does not compare it with the old certificate beyond the checks the router makes.

docs.title: Path segments with special behavior
docs.text:
Request Behavior /.well-known/est/csrattrs/csrattrs Returns the example attributes of RFC 7030 section 4.5.2 /.well-known/est/pkcs7/serverkeygen Returns the key in a CMS SignedData inside an EnvelopedData, encrypted with the pre-shared key pseudohistorical /.well-known/est/triggererrors/... cacerts and csrattrs answer 500. An enrollment with the common name Trigger Error Forbidden answers 403, Trigger Error Deferred answers 202 with Retry-After: 600 and Trigger Error Unknown answers 500

Without a path segment csrattrs returns an empty list.

docs.title: Server-generated keys
docs.text:
/serverkeygen generates an RSA key of 2048 bits. A Bit-Size request header of 2048, 3072 or 4096 selects the size. Any other value answers 400 invalid bit size value:

estclient serverkeygen -server localhost:8443 -explicit anchor.pem -cn device -headers 'Bit-Size:3072' -out cert.pem -keyout key.pem

docs.title: TPM enrollment
docs.text: /tpmenroll issues the certificate as for /simpleenroll and protects it with a 16-byte AES credential, see TPM enrollment.

docs.title: TLS-SRP
docs.text:
The tls_srp section serves the same endpoints on a second port over TLS-SRP (RFC 5054). The client signs in with a username and password in the handshake and needs no trust anchor. The TLS listener keeps running next to it.

{
    "tls_srp": {
        "listen_address": "localhost:8444",
        "verifier_file": "srpvfile"
    }
}
  • listen_address and verifier_file are required. Without them the server stops with failed to start TLS-SRP listener: tls_srp needs listen_address and verifier_file.
  • The listener runs TLS 1.2 with TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA and TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.
  • A TLS-SRP client may run every operation. A renewal needs no client certificate.
  • A failed handshake is logged at info level, such as TLS-SRP handshake from 127.0.0.1:53110 failed: remote error: tls: insufficient security level.

docs.title: The verifier file
docs.text:
The file has the format of openssl srp. Create it and add a user with the 3072-bit group:

touch srpvfile

openssl srp -srpvfile srpvfile -add -gn 3072 device-1

Each line has six tab-separated fields: type, verifier, salt, username, group and info.

  • V lines are users. The group is the size of an RFC 5054 group, such as 3072 or the name of an I line.
  • R lines are revoked users, which openssl srp -delete writes. The server skips them.
  • I lines define a group by its parameters. Only the RFC 5054 groups are accepted.
  • Empty lines and lines that start with # are ignored. A user listed twice, an unknown group or a malformed value stops the server with the line number.

est.Client and other go-tls-srp clients refuse groups below 2048 bits by default. The 1536-bit group that some examples use fails with srptls: server chose the 1536 bit SRP group, below the minimum of 2048 bits.

docs.title: Unknown users
docs.text:
• Without unknown_user_seed, an unknown username fails the handshake with an unknown_psk_identity alert. The client sees srptls: unknown SRP username and learns that the user does not exist.
  • With a seed, an unknown user fails like a wrong password, with srptls: wrong SRP password. The server answers with the group most users in the file have. Keep the seed the same across restarts.
